integ.summary: Theirs is an eleven-skill suite for an anonymous Bachelor's or Master's exposé that ideates, searches, writes, checks, reviews, supervises, customizes, imports, reverses, publishes and troubleshoots, measured by a routing rig and a multi-host eval harness; ours is a four-skill plugin for one course's controlled-experiment proposal that settles and freezes the design, checks the student's own draft item by item against a checklist, and hands off to an external defend stage. Their shipped rules (a five-section exposé, no supervisor names, ethics in two or three sentences, a required Statistical Analysis subsection) conflict with our course, so nothing of theirs should be vendored beyond the lit-search scripts, and their ideas should keep being restated into our checklist. The most valuable things to adopt are cheap: carry an earlier review round forward, re-vendor the scripts at v0.9.0, and add a placeholder report, a cited-versus-listed check and a record of the research questions a review judged. The v3 spec needs correcting before implementation: its scenario 8 would overwrite the four confirmed attestations and the waivers in the author's real proposal/review.md, its planned 429 backoff and output-size signal already exist upstream, its DBLP "defect" is our own query shape, and two frontmatter tests fail for certain under its section 1. We do better on settling and freezing design decisions, experiment and ethics criteria, a checker-validated review with a quote per pass, waivers carried into the defence, and run records tied to a commit; their MIT terms are met, though three of our files overstate how freely the six substance tests were restated.

kept.title: Drafting stage: theirs has an agent writer, ours has none, and our only real use drafted with agents outside the plugin
kept.claim: THEIRS proposal-write writes first drafts and turns bullets into prose: it writes every section, may cite only keys in the references block, marks gaps as [TODO: ...] and re-runs its check before reporting. It also revises against a review. OURS has no first-draft writer. That is a v2 non-goal ("the plugin never writes proposal prose"), and v3 keeps it through its rule that every v2 decision it does not name stands. Our review skill does edit the draft in place, but only for fixes the user picks by number, so the gap is drafting and bullets-to-prose, not revision. The plugin's second use and first full one, the Bloom proposal, was drafted by agents outside the plugin with project-made tools (part files, assemble.py, check.py, apply_edits.py). v3 does not revisit the non-goal in light of that, and its 'Out of scope, considered and rejected' list does not name a writer. The course text says nothing about AI-written prose, so the non-goal is the author's choice, not a course rule. Recommendation stands with one change: re-record the inherited non-goal in v3 together with the new evidence, rather than adding it as a new decision.
kept.recommendation: Keep ours for 0.3.0, but write the decision into v3's 'Out of scope, considered and rejected' list, citing this evidence: real use drafted with agents, and the course does not forbid it. That way the next release revisits it on purpose. If the author later adopts a writer, make it a narrow skill that writes only from the frozen brief into the eight-section skeleton. It should use bracket placeholders for unknowns, cite only sources the user supplied, and have one writer per file, following proposal-write's non-negotiables (restate them; do not vendor). Cost: none now, large if adopted.

kept.title: Idea stage is uncovered, and design (in v3 agent mode too) can supply the study's research question itself
kept.claim: OURS has no separate idea stage. By design (v1 spec line 140, "Given only an idea, it starts from scratch"), `design` turns a raw idea into a research question by treating item 1.1 as an ordinary design-tree item. When the material lacks a question, design offers a model-written `Recommended:` question, and "I don't know" makes it the provisional Decision. Under v3's Agent run, every unanswered frontier item goes provisional. Item 6.1's only design-tree dependency is 1.1 (5.1 is review-only), so an agent-run brief can carry a model-written research question and hypotheses (6.1, 6.2). They are flagged, not silent: they are listed first under Open items, and the brief stays open. THEIRS's proposal-ideate makes origination "the one hard rule": research questions come from the student and are never supplied. research-grill has an `idea` stage (a topic or hunch to one falsifiable research question), but our README and skills name only its defend stage. The course's first deliverable, a one-paragraph outline, is an idea-stage output that falls before the formal-proposal lens the plugin targets.
kept.recommendation: Adopt in OURS plugins/experiment-proposal/skills/design/SKILL.md steps 2-3. When item 1.1 is weak or missing, put no recommendation; ask for the question in the user's words, or stop and print `/oss:research-grill idea`, with the install commands when absent (reuse review's installed_plugins.json detection). Recommendations for items 6.1 and 6.2 must cite a source from the material or from Looked up. In v3 §1 Agent run, a missing 1.1 stops design with that message instead of writing a provisional question. Add one line to the README Commands order naming the idea step.

kept.title: Invocation model: upstream measures description-based routing; v3 tests only that nothing fires unprompted
kept.claim: THEIRS leaves all eleven skills model-invocable with trigger-rich descriptions and measures selection directly. Its dataset has 60 cases (canonical, oblique, collision, negative). The published report covers 58 of them over 3 epochs, 171 of 174 correct, and one oblique proposal-write case misses in 3 of 3 epochs. v3 deliberately makes our four skills callable by name with name-only descriptions, so upstream's canonical and oblique positives have no counterpart here. The comparable parts are by-name positives and the negative and collision half, where upstream has 4 negatives and 14 collisions at 3 epochs each. v3 checks one in-domain lure on Claude Code, 'plan a controlled HCI experiment... what should I do first?', with no skill invoked unprompted in three runs. It also runs a by-name invocation test on Codex, and scenario 8 runs the skills in agent mode on Claude Code without a bar. It has no by-name positive with a bar per skill on Claude Code. It also has no out-of-domain negative or collision utterances that the generic names `design` and `review` could attract once the flag is gone, such as 'review this pull request' or 'design a survey'.
kept.recommendation: Adopt in v3 §5 scenario 7 a small routing set modelled on routing_cases.toml, 3 epochs each, with the author's usual plugin set enabled. Positives: one by-name utterance per skill, expecting that skill. Negatives and collisions, expecting none of ours: 'review this pull request', 'design a survey for my class', 'find papers on transformer pruning', 'help me prepare for my IRB meeting', 'check my essay's word count'. Bar: every positive routes and no negative selects ours.

kept.title: Hand-off and chaining: theirs loads the next skill on 'yes'; ours prints commands, which research-grill requires
kept.claim: THEIRS ends every skill with Where it stands / Next / Or on a four-rung ladder. The lines never name a skill; when the user approves, the agent loads the skill that owns the step. Sibling skills are also composed in place by reading ../<sibling>/SKILL.md. All upstream skills can be invoked by the model. OURS prints exact commands: review prints the defend command, and design's Open items list /experiment-proposal:lit-search. Load-on-approval cannot properly reach our defend stage: research-grill is in another plugin with no sibling path, and it is set to disable-model-invocation: true. In v3's Agent run, "nothing else in the steps changes", so those printed commands survive, and the plugin's own skills become callable by name. What it does not do is name a step for the caller at the three exits only a human can take: approving the freeze of a brief left open, confirming attested items recorded as not confirmed, and running the user-only defend command. lit-search and the-ethics-board just "return their report" with no follow-on step.
kept.recommendation: Keep ours for the research-grill hand-off: a printed command is the only route to a user-invoked skill. In v3 §1, adopt one fixed closing line per Agent run naming the next call for the orchestrator. design: 'brief open, N provisional; the user freezes it with /experiment-proposal:design'. review: the defend command for the user. lit-search: 'add the kept sources to the draft; review attests item 5.2'.

kept.title: Upstream lit-search changed after our pin; the 429 retry already exists and the YAML quoting is unchanged
kept.claim: Since the pin a38b7b1, three commits touched the vendored scripts (b5d24b5, b311e4f, a721bfd). The lit-search SKILL.md changed in four commits; the snowball and candidates-line changes came with b5d24b5. SKILL.md now says to snowball one seed per call. snowball.py still accepts several DOIs, but its --limit-per-seed default fell from 20 to 5. Our SKILL.md still snowballs the best two or three seeds at --limit-per-seed 20, which no longer matches. The two entry scripts, search.py and snowball.py, now print a stderr line 'candidates: N (L lines, C characters on stdout)' so a truncated host display can be detected. Retry on HTTP 429/5xx already existed at the pin and is unchanged at HEAD: 2 retries with linear backoff, 3 s then 6 s. So v3's planned PR should argue for a longer or Semantic Scholar-specific backoff, not add backoff. a721bfd also replaced arXiv's http_text with a classified fetch, which gives arXiv 429/5xx retry; that is one more reason to re-vendor. _yaml_scalar and the title/abstract normalization are unchanged, so titles with embedded newlines are still emitted unquoted upstream. If the planned wrapper relays all vendored stderr verbatim, it will relay the candidates line as if it were a degradation note, unless it filters stderr by line type, as the existing 'sources:' line already requires. N also counts records before --exclude, so it works only as a truncation signal, not as a result count.
kept.recommendation: Adopt before writing litsearch.py: re-vendor the nine scripts at 1666e69 and update the provenance headers and THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES. In the wrapper, parse the candidates line as a count, use it to flag truncation, and keep it out of the relayed notes. Run snowball with one seed per call. Reword the upstream PR to 'quote strings containing newlines; longer 429 backoff for Semantic Scholar'.

kept.title: v3 contradicts itself on whether lit-search writes a file; upstream records rejections only in an existing notes file
kept.claim: v3 contradicts itself on whether lit-search writes a file. §1 keeps "writes no files", SKILL.md step 4 still says "write no files", and the README's Writes column says "nothing". Yet §3 has the judge (the skill, per step 3) append every judged DOI to proposal/notes/lit-search-judged.txt, and its wrapper has an `--out <file>` option. Upstream records only rejections (DOI or title plus a one-line reason) in the Excluded Literature section of a notes.md that already exists. Kept entries are merged into the proposal and deduped against its references block. Upstream also keeps candidate lists in the chat and never creates files for them. So a dedicated judged-file is our own design, not something adopted from upstream. Because our skill never merges kept sources into the draft, the exclude list needs both kept and rejected DOIs. Recommendation as stated, with two additions. First, §3's exclude parse ("one DOI per line") must read only the first field once lines carry a verdict and reason. Second, §1's description, the README's Writes column, SKILL.md's description and step 4 must name the file, and so must `--out`, if kept. Cost: small.
kept.recommendation: Adopt: lit-search writes proposal/notes/lit-search-judged.txt as its one artifact, one line per judged DOI with its verdict (kept or rejected) and a one-line reason, so the file is both the exclude list and the record item 5.2 attests to. Update the v3 §1 description, the README Writes column and SKILL.md step 4 ('write no files').

kept.title: No placeholder or TODO-marker check in our checker; theirs flags every open marker and the author wrote one by hand
kept.claim: THEIRS treats open markers as first-class, but only in its own syntax. check.py:1760 warns (it does not raise an error) on each `[TODO: ...]` match of structure.json's `\[TODO:[^\]]*\]`. Its writing skills produce these markers. publish renders them as numbered callouts with no quiet option, and the proposal-write and proposal-check hand-offs sort them into decisions the student owes and execution details. OURS check_proposal.py, its skills, its checklist and the v3 spec have no placeholder rule of any kind. So a draft containing `[DATA STORAGE LOCATION]` passes the `draft` mechanics, and the author had to write a check that every bracketed placeholder appears in Appendix H (check.py lines 27 and 68-76). Our plugin does not write the draft, so it has no marker convention of its own, and adopting this means picking a pattern. The author's `[NAME]` / `[NAME: gloss]` regex is a ready model. Recommendation: add a `draft --placeholders` report shaped like the planned (spec-only, not yet implemented) `--numbers`. It lists each match with its section and line, judges nothing and exits 0. `review` reads it for item 13.5 and lists the open placeholders in the hand-off. Small cost: `check_draft` already parses headings.
kept.recommendation: Adopt in OURS plugins/experiment-proposal/scripts/check_proposal.py a `draft --placeholders` report. Like v3's --numbers, it lists each bracketed all-caps placeholder with its section and line, judges nothing and exits 0. review reads the report for item 13.5 (a draft to be submitted) and prints the open placeholders in the hand-off seed list. Add it to v3 §2 and its unit tests.

kept.title: Review across rounds: theirs carries the earlier round forward; ours rewrites review.md and loses waivers
kept.claim: THEIRS reads an existing review.md before overwriting it and marks each earlier blocker resolved, partly resolved or open. A finding about an unchanged passage keeps its class or drops to a lower one. The only exception is a title name the earlier round did not hold to the swap test; it can come back as a blocker labelled "missed in the earlier round". The review closes with a verbatim record of the research questions it judged, so check can warn `review-questions-changed` and treat the review as superseded. OURS describes review.md as a record of one pass. Step 5 writes it fresh, and the reference and the checker allow exactly seven sections, so there is no place for an earlier round. When the student revises and runs review again, the user's verbatim waiver reasons and the `(fix N applied)` history from the earlier run are lost, and nothing flags a review that no longer matches the draft. The author's real project went through several review rounds outside the plugin (two methods reviews, a red team, a verification pass), which shows multi-round reviewing is the expected use.
kept.recommendation: Adopt in OURS review step 1: when proposal/review.md exists, read it first. Carry each waiver forward whose quoted passage is unchanged, re-asking only when it changed, and give each earlier fail row a note: 'was fail in <date>: resolved/open'. Allow an optional `## Earlier round` line in references/review.md and the checker. Consider for v3 if scenario 8 includes a second review pass; otherwise 0.4.0.

kept.title: Customization is not persisted, and v3's agent mode silently reverts to the course defaults
kept.claim: THEIRS stores program and supervisor rules in a workspace guidelines.md that its skills read. OURS asks for the item 3.1 values (section list, word bounds, reference bounds, supervisor's name) on every review run and keeps them nowhere: the 3.1 row only has to say `confirmed by the user, <date>`, and the next run does not read the earlier review.md. In v3's agent run, review uses the course defaults at 3.1 and marks the row `not confirmed`. A user who confirmed different values in an earlier interactive review therefore gets the defaults back. Rows 13.5 and 5.1 are then judged against those defaults, and nothing says the earlier values were dropped. The practical impact is limited, because the single course's defaults usually apply and v3's literature-review-only reference count removes the one deviation seen in real use.
kept.recommendation: Adopt the persistence, not the TOML file. The 3.1 row of proposal/review.md records the confirmed values as the exact checker flags (`--sections "..." --words A-B --references A-B --supervisor "..."`). review, interactive or agent-run, offers or uses those values from an existing review.md before the course defaults. Amend v3 §1 accordingly. Keep rejecting a general override file: one course needs no customization surface.

kept.title: Framing conflict: their thesis-exposé rules forbid what our course requires, so adoption means restating, never vendoring
kept.claim: THEIRS targets an anonymous Bachelor's or Master's exposé in English or German, with five required sections: Introduction, Contribution, Research Questions, Methodology and Timeline. The page limit is about 5 (a warning at 500 words per page). The reference floor is 3, but a density advisory of 4 per 1000 words expects 10-15. Its shipped rules forbid supervisor names (guidelines line 43; the check agent flags supervisor references), forbid "supervisor" as a heading, and keep ethics to "two or three precise sentences ... not a compliance appendix". Its Controlled Experiment branch requires a Statistical Analysis subsection. THEIRS does not forbid timelines. Timeline is a required section, kept to one sentence by default, and [timeline] detail = "detailed" allows a full work plan. The course has no timeline section, and our item 2.4 applies only when the template asks for one. The course and OURS require these things THEIRS forbids or omits: eight differently named sections ending in an Appendix; a consent form stating the study is under the named instructor's supervision (item 12.3); an appendix holding the recruiting materials, script, consent form and questionnaires (item 12.1); 2,000-4,000 words; and 15-20 references. Neither the course nor OURS has an analysis section (step 11 dropped), where THEIRS requires Statistical Analysis. Run with defaults on our draft, their check would report required-section-missing for all five canonical headings plus methodology-missing, and their agent passes would flag the supervision sentence and the author name. Customize can override the section list (including an Appendix heading, which also turns off the Statistical Analysis rule), raise page_limit and min_count, and drop "supervisor" from the forbidden headings. It cannot mechanically express the appendix contents, the supervision sentence, a 20-reference ceiling or a word floor; those can only go in free prose. The course also allows an archival or PRISMA track. THEIRS's slr branch is a structural near-match for it (Search Strategy and Selection Criteria, Quality Assessment and Extracted Information, Synthesis) but has no PRISMA guidance. OURS does not cover that track at all.
kept.recommendation: Keep ours. Take further upstream ideas the way the six substance tests were taken, restated into the checklist, and never vendor write, check or review. Add one README sentence: the plugin covers the course's experiment track only, not the archival or PRISMA option.

kept.title: We have the stages they lack: frozen design decisions with an HCI subagent, an ethics rehearsal, and a defend rehearsal
kept.claim: THEIRS has no stage that settles and freezes design decisions. Their ideate skill works out a plausible method through questions, and write picks the methodology when the material leaves it open, marking it [TODO: confirm methodology choice]. write's handoff gives the student up to three owed decisions as anchored choices. Decisions are kept as free text in the Decisions section of notes.md, which write does not re-litigate, but nothing gives them a status, freezes them by commit, or checks them. THEIRS covers controlled-experiment design (variables, confounds, within- or between-subjects design, assignment, validity threats) and human-participant ethics (ethics route, informed consent, data handling, risk) only as unchecked guidance. It explicitly says this "is not a compliance appendix". It has no ethics rehearsal and no consent-form artifact, and nothing rehearses the student's defence: review writes a verdict file, and supervise is the professor's tool. OURS settles design-tree items in rounds and consults hci-researcher on counterbalancing, controls and confounds (items 7.5, 7.7, 7.9). It freezes the brief by commit and changes it only through amendments. It rehearses an ethics board and checks the consent form against the course's requirements (items 12.1, 12.3, 12.4). The defend rehearsal is not part of our plugin: review hands off to research-grill, which the user installs separately. Recommendation: keep ours. These stages enforce the course's experiment and ethics requirements, which THEIRS covers only as unchecked guidance. Do not import supervise.
kept.recommendation: Keep ours: these stages carry the course's experiment-specific and ethics requirements, which THEIRS does not model. Do not import supervise. Its professor-facing feedback has no user in a one-student course, and its workload verdict is already covered by items 2.2 and 2.4.

kept.title: Publishing stage: theirs builds a PDF; ours stops at markdown while the course wants the CHI template
kept.claim: THEIRS proposal-publish builds a compact PDF with pandoc, using typst first, then LaTeX, with docx as the last resort. It also exports a stripped handout and hands over to a proposal-build file in the proposal's folder when one exists. OURS has no publish stage, and its outputs stay Markdown. The course asks for the CHI publication template for both the proposal and the later 3,500 to 6,000-word paper. The author's format doc assigns the port to the author. In real use the author's project built its own WeasyPrint PDF (proposal/notes/build_pdf.py), with four recorded departures from the ACM template. Their built-in typst/LaTeX layout is not the CHI template. Their handover hook could run a CHI-style (acmart) build, but only one the user writes, so adopting their pipeline would not by itself produce a compliant document.
kept.recommendation: No action for 0.3.0. The course's template port is the author's, and no shipped renderer matches the CHI format. Revisit only if a later course deliverable (the 3,500-6,000-word paper in the same template) brings the plugin into scope.

kept.title: Import and reverse-engineering: theirs converts documents; ours extracts decisions and gates review on a brief
kept.claim: THEIRS proposal-import converts an existing PDF, Word or LaTeX proposal into its single-markdown format: it strips personal data, validates references with validate_refs.py and seeds notes.md. proposal-reverse derives a proposal from a finished thesis, either to reconstruct a missing proposal or to build a teaching exemplar. OURS has no document import. A draft in Word, PDF or LaTeX would have to be converted to markdown by hand before check_proposal.py or review could read it. The nearest step is design's extraction, which reads the user's material and marks each design-tree item settled, weak or missing with a quoted passage. That extracts decisions; it does not convert a draft. review refuses to run without a frozen brief. In the real use the brief was back-filled after the draft (draft committed 15 October, brief frozen 17 October). The v3 spec says the cause was the skills being user-invoked only, which made an agent re-run each SKILL.md by hand, not the review gate. The v3 spec plans a scenario 8, not yet run and to be recorded without a bar, that has design extract from docs/study-decisions.md. No action and a cost of none are reasonable for this course, because the author writes the proposal in markdown part files.
kept.recommendation: No action. design's extraction is the import this workflow needs, and scenario 8 covers it. Reverse serves exemplar-building, which the course does not ask for.

kept.title: Troubleshooting: theirs has a diagnosis ladder and a failure offer in every skill; ours has no failure path
kept.claim: THEIRS: proposal-troubleshoot works through a ladder of rungs: stale install, model unable, supervisor override, script failed, mandate violated, output merely disliked. It stops at the first rung that explains the problem. It writes a local bug report only for a failed script (rung 3), a violated mandate (rung 4), or a cause it cannot identify, or as optional evidence against a model (rung 1). Rungs 0, 2 and 5 end with an answer and no report. Ten of the eleven skills, all except proposal-troubleshoot, offer the troubleshoot route once when a run fails. They also say that weak-material findings are the skill working, not a defect. OURS: the skills do have stop conditions: a missing or unfrozen brief, a missing draft, or Python older than 3.11 each stops with a message. But neither the skills, the README nor the v3 spec helps the user tell a skill defect from a weak draft or a failing review row, and none of them says where to report a defect.
kept.recommendation: Adopt minimally: one README paragraph, 'If a skill misbehaves'. It says: update with `claude plugin update experiment-proposal@research-vault`; re-run the checker command the skill names; a failing review row is the skill working; otherwise open an issue in eranroseman/research-vault with the checker output. No troubleshoot skill.

kept.title: Cited-vs-listed cross-check: theirs is code, ours is prose at 3.3, and v3 leaves it out
kept.claim: Their check.py compares cited @keys with the reference IDs in the document's metadata in both directions. An undefined key is an error and an uncited reference is a warning. Our checker never compares the two in either direction. Item 3.3 ('every cited work listed under References') is checked only by the reviewer reading, and the v3 plan parses [n] brackets only to count the literature review's citations. A citation [29] against a 28-entry list, or an entry nobody cites, passes. Adopt it as a check for numbered lists: compare the [n] numbers cited in the body and appendices (outside References) against the [n] entries in the list. A missing entry is a defect feeding item 3.3. An entry nobody cites is an informational line only, because 3.3 covers just the cited-to-listed direction. The number scan needs the same exclusions the v3 count parse needs (code spans, and non-citation numbers such as scale anchors), because rendered [n] is less clear-cut than their @keys. The author-year fallback has no entry numbers to match, so it is out of scope. Cost: small.
kept.recommendation: Adopt. Add two lines to section 2 of the v3 spec and to `check_draft`, reusing the bracket parser v3 already needs. A defect 'citations: [n] cited at line L has no entry n' (n greater than the entry count, or missing from `[n]`-numbered entries), feeding item 3.3. A warning or informational line 'references: entry n is never cited'. Scan the body and appendices outside References. Add both to the v3 unit-test list.

kept.title: v3 --numbers would report citation numbers as values; upstream has no equivalent check
kept.claim: Nothing in the upstream code checks whether numbers agree across sections. proposal-review leaves 'inconsistencies between sections' to the agent reading under Sharpness, so v3 `--numbers` has no upstream equivalent. The spec's rule matches any number within six words of a keyword and masks nothing. On the current proposal.md, the saved simulation skips References and finds 286 number tokens near a keyword (168 distinct tokens). 17 of them are numeric citation brackets, e.g. '[20], and Bloom's participants'. The report would list them as values under participants (5), % (5), items (4), and min, session and minutes. Section headings also produce false hits: '## 4 Participants' puts 4 next to the keyword. Upstream has one reusable technique for this: mask_code blanks code spans and fences while keeping offsets. Its bracket-depth loop sorts [@key] citations into bracketed and author-in-text, so it does not apply to [n] numbers. Recommendation: keep the report. Before matching, blank [n] brackets, inline code and heading numbers without shifting offsets. State outright that References is not scanned. The spec's word-count row already treats references as separate from the body, so a separate rule for four-digit years is only needed if References is scanned. Add a fixture with a citation bracket planted next to 'participants' and assert that it is not listed. Cost: small.
kept.recommendation: Keep the v3 report (we-have-they-lack once shipped). Amend the spec: blank `[n]` citation brackets, inline code, and heading numbering (e.g. '7 Design', 'C.2') before matching, as their mask_code does, without shifting offsets. Also exclude four-digit years in the reference list. Add a planted citation bracket next to 'participants' to the v3 fixture and assert that it is not listed.

kept.title: v3 informational lines have no output channel; their findings carry a level and only errors fail
kept.claim: Our checker's contract is defects only. Text mode prints `<file>:<line>: <message>` lines, `--json` prints a list of defects, and exit is 1 whenever that list is non-empty. The v3 spec adds the informational line `references: <N> entries in the list` without naming its stream (stdout or stderr) or its place in `--json`. An implementer who routes it through the Defect list makes every draft fail, and the review skill would file it under item 5.1. For `draft --numbers` the spec does name stdout and says `--json` is honored. It does not give the JSON shape, and it does not say whether "Exit 0 always" overrides the exit 1 from draft defects when both run in one call. Their checker avoids this: each finding carries a level ("error" or "warning"), only errors set exit 1, and the JSON is an object that wraps the findings with an exit_code field.
kept.recommendation: Adopt the minimum. The v3 spec should send informational lines to stderr, which matches the existing frozen-brief note our checker already prints there, so stdout and `--json` stay defects only. Give `--numbers` its own JSON object shape. Alternatively add a `level` field to Defect and count only `defect` toward exit 1. Choose one in the spec before implementing.

kept.title: DOI and title verification against Crossref (validate_refs.py); ours has none
kept.claim: Their proposal-import and proposal-reverse skills (not write, check or supervise) run validate_refs.py. For each entry with a DOI, it looks the DOI up on Crossref. If the entry has a title, it checks that the returned title matches after normalization. An entry without a DOI goes to a Crossref title search, and only an exact normalized-title match among the top 5 results is accepted. It edits nothing. It prints VERIFIED / ENRICHED / UNVERIFIABLE / OFFLINE for each entry and tells the agent to add `[TODO: verify reference id]`. Our plugin never checks that a listed reference exists: check_proposal.py counts entries, and item 5.1 checks coverage and the count, so a fabricated or wrong-DOI entry passes both. The check cannot go into check_proposal.py, which v3 keeps network-free, so it would be a separate script. The pinned version (a38b7b1) uses only functions our vendored common.py and crossref.py already have. HEAD (b311e4f) also calls common.utf8_output(), which our copy lacks. Its extractor reads a CSL-YAML `references:` block, so we would need a parser for ACM `[n]` lines. Pulling out the DOI takes a regex, but it must allow parentheses (e.g. 10.1016/S0166-4115(08)...). Pulling the title out of ACM prose is the hard part and the reason the cost is medium. 24 of the 28 real entries have a doi.org URL. The other 4 (a questionnaire, a book, an unpublished manual, an arXiv/COLM paper) will likely come back UNVERIFIABLE from the title search, which is expected and not a defect. The nine-scripts test (line 273), which globs every *.py in skills/lit-search/scripts, has to be updated to allow the new script; v3's planned litsearch.py in the same folder already breaks it. The environment-name scan at line 346 also globs that folder but only collects names, so it does not need to change.
kept.recommendation: Adopt as our own `skills/lit-search/scripts/verify_refs.py` (not vendored). It imports the vendored common and crossref modules, parses `[n]` lines for the DOI and title, and prints VERIFIED / UNVERIFIABLE / OFFLINE per entry. `review` runs it for item 5.1 when the network is available. Update the nine-scripts test, which globs every *.py in that folder: it must admit verify_refs.py, and v3's planned litsearch.py in the same folder already breaks it.

kept.title: Leftover TODO/placeholder markers: they warn and render them visibly; our checker passes them
kept.claim: Their check warns (warning level, still exit 0) on every `[TODO: ...]` marker, and their PDF build renders leftover `[TODO: ...]` markers as numbered annotations so a gap cannot pass for finished prose. Their rule matches only that exact syntax, so `[TBD]` or all-caps placeholders such as `[DATA STORAGE LOCATION]` would go unreported in their tool too. Our draft checker has no placeholder rule of any kind and reports nothing, so a draft full of placeholders exits 0 with no output. The author's project had to add its own check that bracketed placeholders in the text equal the Appendix H list. Adopting this means a broader pattern than theirs (TODO, TBD and all-caps brackets), plus an optional comparison against a named list heading.
kept.recommendation: Adopt in `check_draft`: list each `[TODO...]`, `[TBD...]` and all-caps bracketed placeholder with its line, at warning or informational level per checks-3, feeding item 13.5 ('the draft to be submitted'). Add an optional `--placeholders "<heading>"` flag that compares the set with the list under that heading, as the author's check.py does.

kept.title: Every RQ referenced in the method section: an error in theirs, prose in our 13.10
kept.claim:
Their check numbers research questions by position in an ordered list ("1." or "1)") in the research-questions section. It errors when the literal token `(RQn)`, parentheses included, is missing from the single methodology section. Their write skill enforces a matching convention: one `(RQn)` at the end of each sentence that answers the question. Our item 13.10 asks for the same link, but only the `review` reader judges it, and neither check_proposal.py nor the v3 spec has any label check.

Their exact rule does not carry over. Our proposal lists RQ1-RQ4 as "- **RQ1:**" bullets, which their rule rejects with research-questions-not-a-list. Our Design section tags labels inline, as "(RQ1, the single confirmatory outcome)" and "(RQ3 measures the latter)", so even with an ordered list the literal match would flag RQ1 and RQ3 although they are referenced. Only (RQ2) and (RQ4) match literally. The port should therefore match bare `RQ\d+` / `H\d+[a-z]?` labels.

The scope should be the union of Materials, Procedure and Design, not Design alone, since 13.10 judges those three sections together. Procedure lacking RQ2 and RQ4 is not a 13.10 defect. On the real proposal all four labels appear in Design, so the check would print nothing: it guards future drafts and found nothing in this one. Our checker has no warning level, so "warning" means an informational line like v3's `--numbers` output or its reference-list total. The hypothesis half is untested because the proposal declares no hypotheses.
kept.recommendation: Adopt as a warning, not a defect: collect `RQ\d+` and `H\d+[a-z]?` labels from the section matching the third `--sections` name and report each one absent from the Design section, with the line where it is defined. `review` reads the list for items 13.10 and 7.x. Skip silently when no labels are defined.

kept.title: Since the pin, check.py grew ~750 lines; review currency is the only rule that applies to us
kept.claim: Four upstream commits since a38b7b1 touch check.py, for a net growth of about 680 lines (719 insertions, 37 deletions; 756 lines changed). Two of them, b5d24b5 and e77314f, account for 775 gross insertions (e77314f also deletes 273 lines). They enforce the per-proposal folder and companion-file family and add checks for which guidelines applied and for unused build definitions. None of this fits our fixed proposal/ folder. b311e4f makes script output UTF-8. That fix is marginally relevant to us: check_proposal.py:284 echoes heading text from the brief, which can fail to print on non-UTF-8 consoles such as Windows (Codex hosts are best-effort). a3f654e adds `review-questions-changed`, an advisory warning that never changes the exit code. Upstream's sha256 report digest is older than the pin, not a new addition. Our review.md names the draft by path only, so nothing detects a review left stale by later edits. Recommendation: the digest is still a small change, but it needs three adjustments. (a) It should only inform, never flag a defect, since upstream rejected hashing because every polishing edit would trigger it. (b) Step 6 must rewrite the digest after it applies fixes. (c) To catch an agent run that edited the draft, take the digest when the draft is read in step 1, not when review.md is written.
kept.recommendation: Adopt the digest variant, which suits our whole-draft review better than an RQ record. `review` writes `Draft: <path> (sha256 <12 hex>)`. `check_proposal.py review` reports to stderr when the named draft's current digest differs, as information and not a defect. The v3 agent-run rule 'applies no fixes' becomes checkable by comparing the digest before and after. Ignore the folder and family rules.

kept.title: Stable rule ids in JSON: they key on ids; we key on English messages
kept.claim: Their check.py findings carry a stable `rule` id from a closed RULE_IDS set alongside the message. The fixture oracles assert the exact set of fired rule ids (and also message fragments). Some JSON-reachable verdicts (verdict_no_orphans, the unit-tested disallowed_rules) key on rule ids. Their sandboxed eval scorers (verdict_draft, the import verdict) still match English fragments such as 'references — at least', so they are only partly protected against rewording. Our Defect JSON has only path, line and message. The review skill routes checker lines to items 3.2, 13.5, 5.1, 4.3 and 12.3 by an informal message prefix (sections:, words:, references:, introduction:, appendix:). Our tests mostly assert message substrings. v3 rewords the references message and adds new ones without adding a rule or item field. Adding `rule` and `item` fields to Defect and its JSON would turn the informal prefix into a real contract, at small cost.
kept.recommendation: Adopt in v3: add `item` (the owning checklist id) and `rule` (e.g. `draft-words`, `draft-lit-citations`) fields to Defect and to the JSON. The review SKILL then says 'each line goes to its item field'. Tests assert on rule and item, with message text checked in one place.

kept.title: Their reference count does not implement the v3 literature-review count
kept.claim: The direct question has a negative answer. Their reference checks count the entries in the metadata block (a floor of 3) and scale an advisory expectation by the body's word count (4 per 1000 words). Neither counts citations inside a section, and neither handles numeric citations. The v3 section-scoped count of distinct `[n]` in the Literature Review is our own design with no upstream code to borrow. Their density idea does not fit a lens with fixed bounds of 15 to 20.
kept.recommendation: Keep ours (the v3 plan as written, plus checks-1). Port nothing from their reference counting.

kept.title: Word-count definitions differ by ~80 words on the real draft, which sits 3 words under the limit
kept.claim: Their single body-word definition drops heading lines. Ours counts every token before References outside the appendices, including headings, the title block and tables. On the real proposal our checker reports 3997 words against a 4000 limit. The same text gives 3920 without headings, 3866 without tables as well, and 3855 without `[n]` citations too. v3 keeps ours as the conservative reading, which is safe (it never under-reports), but the 3-word margin means the README note matters.
kept.recommendation: Keep ours. In the v3 README sentence on word count, say that headings and tables add roughly 2 to 4% over a prose-only count, so a draft near the bound can ask the instructor which reading applies.

kept.title: Fixture oracles: their expected.json per fixture vs our inline asserts and a prose answer key
kept.claim: Each of their fixtures has an expected.json with the exit code, message fragments and the exact rule ids for errors and warnings. Two parametrized tests check every oracle against the script. Our one draft fixture (proposal-with-defects.md) is pinned by a single test in tests/test_experiment_proposal_checker.py that asserts exit 1 and three exact message strings. Most of our draft-checker tests are synthesized valid_draft() mutations, including the parametrized old/new/message table, not fixture files. The evals' answer key is a prose table scored by hand. In the v3 spec, only `--numbers` gets a fixture (one planted mismatch, and it always exits 0). The `[n]`-entry and literature-review-count behaviours are specified as unit tests, which fit the existing valid_draft() pattern. An expected.json oracle (exit code plus rule ids) is only worth adding if checks-8 adds rule ids. Even then it would cover one or two fixture files, so its value is small.
kept.recommendation: Adopt only if checks-8 lands. Write `proposal-with-defects.expected.json` (exit code plus rule and item ids) and one parametrized test over all draft fixtures, so the v3 fixtures are added as data rather than as new assert blocks. Without rule ids, keep the current tests.

kept.title: Hindsight-leakage heuristic (results stated as already obtained) vs our prose 'future tense' rule
kept.claim: Their hindsight-leakage rule (check.py lines 1864-2109) flags a sentence only if it cites nothing and does not continue a cited sentence through a back-reference such as "they" or "their ...". Such a sentence is flagged when it contains a result verb ('showed', 'demonstrated', ...), or when it contains a change word anywhere alongside a number with %/percent. The change word does not have to be next to the number. Present-tense passives ('is demonstrated') count as plans and are not flagged. The rule stops at the first hit, so a draft gets at most one warning. About 120 lines are specific to this rule: regex constants for English and German (attribution cues, reporting clauses, expletive 'it') and three functions. Another ~95 lines split text into sentences while handling abbreviations and ordinals, and the citation-repeated rule shares them. They added the rule for their proposal-reverse skill, which turns a finished thesis into a proposal; our plugin has no such skill, so the main case it guards against does not arise for us. Our item 3.3 requires the future tense but leaves the check to the reviewer, and nothing in our checker or the v3 spec checks tense. Recommendation: no action for v3. Revisit only if a later eval plants a past-tense result claim and `review` passes it. Scenario 5 plants no such defect and treats 3.3 as a control expected to pass, so it cannot fire this trigger as written. A pilot that reports real results ('we found ... reduced ... 20%') would also trip the rule, and item 8.1 allows reporting pilot data.
kept.recommendation: No action for v3. Revisit, as an English-only warning feeding 3.3 (adopting would be medium cost), only if a scenario-5 run passes a planted past-tense result claim. A pilot that reports real results would also trip it.

kept.title: PDF build and CI-built documents: theirs builds and tests real PDFs; we build nothing
kept.claim: Their publish skill builds the proposal through pandoc and citeproc into typst, LaTeX or docx, using a compact numeric CSL. Their CI builds every fixture in pinned pandoc/typst and pandoc/extra (LaTeX) containers. Their separate Windows job runs only the fast test subset, with no document builds. Our plugin ships no build. Our CI covers it with pytest and pre-commit lint (plus repo-wide crap4py, drywall and a mutation gate on research_vault), and none of these builds a document. The lens requires the CHI 2025 format, which their templates (proposal.typ, compact-numeric.csl) do not produce. The author's project already has its own build_pdf.py (pandoc to HTML, then WeasyPrint).
kept.recommendation: No action for v3. A CHI (acmart) build is large work, and their pipeline cannot be reused for it.

kept.title: Shape checks of review.md and the brief: ours recomputes them; theirs has nothing comparable
kept.claim: Our checker (check_proposal.py review/brief) validates the shape of review.md and design-brief.md every time it runs, and the review and design skills must reach exit 0 before they finish. For review.md it checks that each checklist item has one row, in order. A draft-checked pass needs a quoted passage with its location, and an attested pass needs `confirmed by the user, <date>`. Fixes must be numbered in order of first appearance with no gaps, except numbers covered by `(fix N applied)` markers. Waivers must match the `fail (waived)` rows, and the Summary counts are recomputed from the rows. For the brief it checks the sections, the entry and amendment grammar, and the freeze rules. Their run-time check.py reads review.md only for its research-questions record (the review-questions-changed warning). It classifies notes.md by its headings without validating them, and their proposal-review skill runs no checker on the review it writes. Their dev harness does assert review shape: a tier phrase in the opening lines, the readiness sections, enumerated blockers, earlier-round resolved counts, the verbatim RQ record and named substance tests, plus a workload table and a verification line for supervise. These assertions are made against eval fixtures with known expected outcomes, not on users' reviews, and none of them recomputes summary counts or requires a per-item quote or user confirmation. Recommendation: keep ours. The `not confirmed` result for attested rows is planned in the v3 spec and is not yet implemented.
kept.recommendation: Keep ours. These checks are where the v2 reviews found their defects. The v3 `not confirmed` result extends the same row grammar.

kept.title: Their rules for their own format and their repo hooks do not carry over
kept.claim: Many of their rules enforce their own file format or their institution's rules, not the course's. These include the trailing-YAML metadata block and reference-key shape, the empty References heading, timeline shape (no table or list, at most 3 lines), forbidden headings (work plan, expected results, supervisor), first-person pronouns, email or matriculation numbers, confidentiality markers, and title tells. Some of these work against our lens, not just miss it. The course's section list has no Timeline section, but checklist items 2.4 and 13.11 call for a timeline that names phases and dates when the template asks for one. Their one-sentence, at-most-3-lines timeline would fail that. The CHI author block names the author, and the consent form must name the supervising instructor and give contacts (item 12.3), which collides with their forbidden supervisor heading and forbidden email address. Their pre-commit hook runs sync_shared.py --check over every generated output. That covers five synced copies of check.py, plus the copies of structure.json, guidelines.md, the lit-search scripts, validate_refs.py and model-support.json, the SKILL.md blocks, the install-prompt docs and .gitattributes. We keep one checker and generate no copies. Their pre-push hook refuses pushes from a shell with no terminal, which is a guard for the maintainer's own releases. No action; our --sections order check covers what their required-section and section-order rules do for our lens.
kept.recommendation: No action. Our `--sections` order check already covers what their required-section and section-order rules do for our lens.

kept.title: v3 agent mode overwrites earlier attestations and waivers; no earlier-round rule
kept.claim: Our review has no rule for a proposal/review.md that already exists. Step 5 writes the file fresh on every pass, and only step 6 records Waivers, from the current pass's answers. So even an interactive re-run drops the earlier verbatim waiver reasons and the fix history unless the user gives them again. v3's Agent run makes this silent and wider. The agent workflow the spec records is an orchestrating agent re-running each SKILL.md, and scenario 8 runs agent-mode review on the author's project, whose review.md already holds four `confirmed by the user` rows. Such a run (a) turns those rows into `not confirmed`, (b) leaves Waivers as `- none`, with no human to waive again, so item 13.5 and the seed list lose them, and (c) takes the course defaults at item 3.1, which throws away any template values the user confirmed and runs the draft checker with the wrong bounds. Nothing stops it from re-failing unchanged text either. Upstream's proposal-review reads the earlier review.md before it overwrites it, judges each earlier blocker against what it asked for, never moves a finding about unchanged text to a higher class, and labels any other new blocker "missed in the earlier round". The recommendation should also carry the confirmed 3.1 values forward into the checker run. Cost is medium mainly because review/SKILL.md (998 of 1,100 words, a cap only a spec edit can move) must absorb both this rule and the Agent run paragraph.
kept.recommendation: Adopt in v3 section 1 and skills/review/SKILL.md step 1. When proposal/review.md exists, read it first. Carry its Waivers and its `confirmed by the user` rows forward; agent mode never downgrades them to `not confirmed`. Mark each earlier fail resolved or open against what its fix asked for. A new fail on text the revision left unchanged carries "missed in the earlier round". Add to v3 scenario 8: an agent-mode re-run after an interactive run keeps the attestations and waivers.

kept.title: Fail verdicts get no evidence rule and no second check
kept.claim: When our review fails an Items row (step 3), it needs only one sentence on what is missing plus a fix: no location, no proof that it searched, and no second check. Cross-section and Brief-against-draft fails already have to name both values and both locations. In their plugin, proposal-supervise (not proposal-review) requires a search that includes synonyms before anything is called absent, and it always runs one fresh verifier with references/verifier-brief.md over the feedback draft. Their proposal-review keeps helper agents out and only caps an adversarial check of fail verdicts at one when a host adds one. Their supervise run's record counts 13 of about 45 confirmed problems as planned work reported missing or quotes cut short. Our own evals show the same failure once, in review-3 (commit 16f7bb6): item 10.3 failed as "never named" when the Procedure does name the program and display. review-v2-1's 8.3 over-failure was a real tension in the fixture, not a false absence. Recommendation: (a) in step 3, a fail that claims absence names the sections it searched, synonyms included. (b) Add one fresh-context checker (Read and Grep only) that re-checks the fail and pass-narrowly rows against the draft. Give it a short brief of our own modelled on check 1 of their verifier brief, and cap it at one checker. Using hci-researcher for this would stretch its role, since its description says "Not for unprompted use" and it advises on design rather than verifying quotes. That review never consults hci-researcher is true but a separate gap.
kept.recommendation: Adopt in skills/review/SKILL.md, in two parts. (a) Step 3: a fail that asserts absence names the sections it searched, synonyms included. (b) A new step between steps 5 and 6: one fresh-context subagent with Read and Grep only re-checks the fail and pass-narrowly rows against the draft and returns its disputes, and review decides on each. For the step 7 to 10 rows, hci-researcher can be that checker; this needs a marked local edit to its routing description. Otherwise use a short brief file of our own. Keep their cap of one verifier, never one per item.

kept.title: Upstream added a review-currency record after our pin; review.md has no staleness marker
kept.claim: Upstream had already made the currency of a review an agent judgement before our pin. Every hand-off block already said "A review whose research questions, scope, method, contribution delta or blocker passages no longer match the text is superseded". After our pin, a3f654e (2026-10-14) added three things. The review now ends with a visible `## Research questions reviewed` record, the proposal's numbered RQs copied word for word. check.py raises the warning `review-questions-changed` (exit code unchanged) when the record and the normalized current RQs differ, and it reports only which positions changed. The proposal-check status read now counts that warning as making the review superseded. Our plugin has neither the judgement rule nor the mechanical check. The review.md header (Brief path with freeze date, Draft path with provenance, Date, Checklist version) records nothing about what the draft said. Nothing tells us when a draft was edited after its review, and the v3 spec's change to the `review` subcommand (`not confirmed`) adds no such check. The recommendation needs correcting, because upstream rejected digests on purpose: a hash fires on every polishing edit and cannot say what changed. A whole-draft sha256 would also go stale as soon as review step 6 applies fixes the user picked, unless step 6 recomputes it. So it would be closer to upstream to record the draft's RQs or hypotheses word for word in review.md, and have `check_proposal.py review` (or `draft`) print an informational line when they differ. That is still a small cost.
kept.recommendation: Adopt in v3 section 2. The review.md header gains a `Draft digest: sha256:<hex>` line. `check_proposal.py review` prints one informational line when the draft named in `Draft:` no longer matches the digest, and the hand-off then says a fresh review is due. It is a warning, not a defect, and the exit code is unchanged.

kept.title: Our review evals never test a hollow or a clean proposal
kept.claim: Their review evals include a mechanically clean but generic proposal that must open with the no-viable-core verdict and name two or more substance tests, and a viable proposal where any blocker counts as overblocking. Our only review fixture is the 12-defect proposal. Its key plants no defect on substance tests 13.6 to 13.11 and lists none of them among the 38 controls. So the substance tests have never been scored against a key, either on a proposal built to fail them or as controls that must pass. Their misfires go unscored: 13.9 failed unplanted in runs review-v2-4 and v2-5 and was counted neither way. Over-failure is measured, but only on the 38 checklist control rows of the defect fixture (at most two allowed), never on a whole proposal meant to pass. v3 scenario 8 states an expected result for review on the author's real proposal ("expect 65 of 65 with four not confirmed") but no bar. Recommendation: add a hollow fixture whose key expects fails on 13.6, 13.7 and 13.8, and a clean fixture whose key expects no fails, 13.6 to 13.11 included. A cheaper partial step is to make 13.6 to 13.11 controls on the existing fixture and to turn scenario 8's expected result into a bar.
kept.recommendation: Adopt in the evals folder, with two fixtures. (1) A hollow fixture: steps 1 to 12 satisfiable, but generic contributions, an unfalsifiable hypothesis and a decorative system name; its key expects fails on 13.6, 13.7 and 13.8. (2) A clean fixture whose key expects zero fails, setting an over-failure bar. Add both to v3 section 5 or to the next release.

kept.title: Our restated swap test lacks their pass conditions for named systems and leaves the title out of scope
kept.claim: For named tools, systems and domains, their swap test spells out what dependence means. A name passes if it is the object of study, imposes constraints that shape the method, supplies data or access no comparable alternative offers, or is the case the proposal argues for. The check is to swap or drop the name and compare claims, not nouns. Prior work, tools that only carry out the method, and domains named only in the motivation are excluded. The title is in scope. Our 13.8 states dependence only as a fail condition ('a named device, system or domain the study does not depend on'). It gives no anchors and no exclusions, and it covers only the overview, the hypotheses and the contributions. The author's run passed 13.8 and cited CARE and MITI, measurement instruments that upstream's rule would exclude, as things the study depends on. It never examined the domain named in the title ('LLM Physical-Activity Coach'). With the anchors, the pass would have had to rest on Bloom's prompts and onboarding states, tied to a specific anchor. Recommendation: in references/checklist.md, add to 13.8 the anchors (in our own words), the exclusion of method instruments and prior work, and the title.
kept.recommendation: Adopt in references/checklist.md item 13.8, in our own words: a named system passes when it is what the study is about, constrains the method, or supplies data or access no comparable alternative offers; the title is held to the same test. Keep the restatement credit in the Deviations section.

kept.title: Three readiness classes with a deferral record versus our pass/fail rows and waivers
kept.claim: They sort every finding into blocker, clarify-early or optional. The reviewer may defer a finding only when its five-field deferral record can be filled, and the fifth field asks whether a bad outcome would force a return to the proposal, naming a fallback if so. A proposal with no blocker is ready. We give each item pass, pass narrowly, fail or fail (waived); items 13.2 and 13.3 always read not checked. Item 13.5 passes only when every item of steps 1 to 12 passes or is waived. A waiver is the user's choice not to fix a failure. Its entry records the item ID, the user's reason and the date, but never what happens if the waived risk comes true. Adopting the fallback field means changing the Waivers shape in references/review.md and the waiver step (step 6) in skills/review/SKILL.md, so that the fallback is asked of the user. A checker clause is needed only if the field is to be enforced, because the current regex matches just the ID prefix.
kept.recommendation: Keep our row results: the course grades every section, so every item is a condition, and 13.5 is our readiness gate. Adopt one field from their deferral record into the Waivers entry shape in references/review.md and the checker's regex: what happens if the waived risk materialises (`; if it bites: <fallback>`). Carry it into the hand-off seed list.

kept.title: No work-package estimate behind the executability judgement
kept.claim: Before the tier, upstream's proposal-supervise skill (not its proposal-review skill) builds a workload table: one row per work package with its dependency, its size driver and a coarse estimate in weeks. Unstated sizes become questions or clarify-early items, and the table closes with a `Scope verdict: fits / tight / over-scoped` line. Our time checks (items 2.2, 2.4, 2.5 and the time clause of 13.11) ask only that the session estimate and the phase timeline fit the time available, and they never ask what drives each phase's size. In the author's run, 13.11 passed because the schedule's milestone dates fell before the 3 December deadline. No phase was sized: not the build, not the pilot sessions, not the MITI coding.
kept.recommendation: Adopt a light version in skills/review/SKILL.md step 4. The 13.11 row's evidence lists each phase from item 2.4 with its size driver (sessions, coding, build) and names any size the draft leaves unstated; a tight fit reads `pass narrowly`. No new section and no checker change. Take no action if the 1,100-word budget for review/SKILL.md cannot absorb it.

kept.title: Supervisor reading and Socratic stance versus our item-by-item pass with quotes
kept.claim: Their proposal-review reads the draft as a supervisor would and gives a three-tier verdict followed by findings, ordered by severity within blocker, clarify-early and optional sections. Each finding carries a concrete actionable suggestion. A separate supervisor-side skill, proposal-supervise, drafts a professor's feedback to a student. It allows at most five blocker points, written in the student's vocabulary rather than review terms, and each gives a direction rather than a prescribed fix. The direction-versus-fix contrast is therefore between their supervise and our review, not between the two reviews. Their Socratic persona appears only in ideation, never in review. Ours checks every item. No item checked against the draft passes without a verbatim quote; attested items pass on `confirmed by the user, <date>`. Every failure carries a ready-to-paste fix or a `decide:` line. The `Next:` line of their review's chat hand-off frames a choice only the student can make as an anchored choice. It quotes the passage, says what the choice changes, offers at most three options from the student's material, and ends with "or something else". Our `decide:` fixes, which sit in review.md fix rows, have no such shape.
kept.recommendation: Keep our item-by-item pass: the lens is an assignment graded section by section, and scenario 5's 12-of-12 rests on the quote rule. Socratic ideation is replaced by design's frontier rounds with recommended answers. Adopt their anchored-choice shape for `decide:` fixes in references/review.md: quote the passage, say what the choice changes, offer at most three options drawn from the user's material, and end with "or something else".

kept.title: How each handles picked fixes, waivers and re-checks
kept.claim: Their review never applies a finding. The user chooses what to apply in the handoff (blockers by name, refinements "by number" as an Or: line), and proposal-write applies them as a separate writing step. A fresh review then reads the earlier round so the findings do not keep growing. Their verdict is advisory, and they have no waivers. The nearest things are proposal-write's per-item report in chat of why an item was skipped, and the reviewer-assigned clarify-early deferral records kept in notes.md Open Points. Neither keeps the user's own refusal reason or passes it to a later stage. Our review applies the fixes the user picks by number in the same pass. It re-checks the touched items, item 13.5, and the Cross-section and Brief sections when a fix touched one of their findings, and marks those rows `(fix N applied)`. A fix the user refuses becomes a `fail (waived)` row plus a Waivers entry with the user's reason verbatim and the date, and each waiver goes into the defend-stage seed list. This holds only for interactive runs: under the v3 spec, an agent run of review applies no fixes and only returns the file path and the Summary line.
kept.recommendation: Keep ours. The plugin has no writing skill (the v2 spec lists "A `draft` writer" as a non-goal), so applying picked fixes inside review, with an in-pass re-check, is the only route. Waivers carry the user's reasons into the defend stage, which an advisory verdict cannot do. No action beyond review-2's carry-forward.

kept.title: Experiment-specific criteria we check that their Controlled Experiment contract does not
kept.claim: Their Controlled Experiment contract is three compressed subsections. It asks for random assignment or a justified quasi-design, but never for a named random source. Their human-participants guidance is advisory and never mechanically checked, and their review blocks only when an indispensable ethics approval is in doubt. We check, item by item: a named random source for assignment (7.4), counterbalancing (7.5), speed paired with accuracy (7.6), group sizes as multiples of the orders (8.8), identical instructions across conditions (10.4), every consent disclosure (12.3), and a point for questions in the script (12.5). The supervision sentence is also checked mechanically by check_proposal.py. Their required Statistical Analysis subsection stays out under our lens. No action needed.
kept.recommendation: Keep ours. Their Statistical Analysis subsection (planned tests, significance level) stays dropped under the v2 Planned Analysis decision, because the lens's section list has none. No action.

kept.title: They check RQ cross-references and tense mechanically; we leave both to the reader
kept.claim: Their guidelines require each research question to be cited as (RQn) in the methodology. Their checker raises an error when the literal "(RQn)" never appears in the methodology section. It also raises a warning (first hit only) when a result verb or change word, such as showed, demonstrated or reduced, appears in a sentence that neither cites a source nor continues a cited one. That is a heuristic for results stated as already obtained, not a general tense check. We judge method fit (item 13.10) and the future-tense convention (item 3.3) by reading only, and v3's `--numbers` keyword list does not include H<n> or RQ<n> labels. Optional adopt: extend `--numbers` to list each H<n>/RQ<n> label with the sections it appears in, as data for the 13.10 row (and 6.x where useful), not for 9.2, which concerns dependent variables in Materials. It still judges nothing. Skip hindsight-leakage because it is a judging regex heuristic, which goes against v3's rule that the checker reports and only a reader judges. v3's explicit rejection covers regexes on declared number constants, not regexes in general.
kept.recommendation: Optional adopt in v3 section 2: extend `--numbers` to list each H<n> or RQ<n> label with the sections it appears in, as data for the 13.10 and 9.2 rows; it still judges nothing. Skip hindsight-leakage: it is a regex heuristic of the kind v3 already rejected.

kept.title: Generic Where-it-stands/Next ladder versus our research-grill defend command
kept.claim: Their review ends each stopping point with Where it stands, Next and at most two Or lines, and the lines never name a skill. The Next step is routed by verdict (revise the blockers then review again, final check then hand-in, or rework the idea). When the user approves, the skill that owns the step is loaded; if it is not installed, the hand-off says so and describes the step in prose. Ours ends every pass with the exact research-grill command (/oss:research-grill defend <draft>). When research-grill is absent, it prints the two install commands before that command. A seed list follows: each waiver, the fixed question "could someone run a session from the Method alone?", and each narrow substance-test pass with its doubt; v3 adds the open ethics revisions. This serves checklist items 13.2 and 13.3, which review deliberately leaves not checked. The difference comes from how the two are packaged: research-grill is an external plugin that is deliberately not declared as a dependency, so ours has to print exact commands rather than load the next skill itself. Keep ours. Scenario 6 holds the hand-off at 0.2.0 after the in-version fix in commit 76e9c28, which re-reads the plugin file before every print. Runs 4 to 6 passed, with one flag on run 5; runs 1 to 3 at 5e13529 failed the absent case. No action, no cost.
kept.recommendation: Keep ours. The defend stage is a separate plugin the user installs, so the exact command is what the hand-off is for, and scenario 6 holds it at 0.2.0. No action.

kept.title: Their six substance tests are unchanged since our pin
kept.claim: Upstream has not changed shared/guidelines/guidelines.md, which defines the six substance tests, or its generated references/ copies since a38b7b1, and that commit is still the file's last change. Five later commits touch the review skill, the supervise skill or shared/, and none of them changes the six tests. They are b5d24b5 (one naming scheme for a proposal's files, which led to the folder layout), b311e4f (UTF-8 script output in check.py), a3f654e (the research-question record), e77314f (the folder layout) and 67dedad (a 0.9.0 version stamp). Our item 13.8 already carries the one-line named-tool clause that a38b7b1 added to the swap test, though not the long dependence paragraph that came with it.
kept.recommendation: No action. Our restatement does not need re-syncing, and the credit in THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md and checklist.md stands. Refinements to the restatement are in review-6.

kept.title: DBLP 'returns nothing' comes from our query shape, not an upstream defect; drop the planned issue
kept.claim: DBLP's empty results on 17 October came from our query shape, not an upstream defect. All six keyword runs (four distinct queries of 6 to 8 terms, plus reruns kw2b and kw3b) got HTTP 200 JSON with @total 0 and no degradation note. DBLP ANDs every space-separated term as a case-insensitive prefix over title, author and venue, and holds no abstracts. Probes today show this directly: health coach gives 178 hits and health coach empathy gives 0, while 2-to-3-term forms return hits. Upstream's live probe sends the one-word query "pentest", so it never covers this case, and neither SKILL.md gives guidance on query length. Recommended spec change: drop the DBLP issue from the Decisions table and §3. The spec text says "three" queries, but there were four. Also reword spec line 10 ("DBLP returned nothing to any query") so the Why section no longer lists it as a degradation. The caller has to supply the short DBLP query, either through SKILL.md step 3 or a wrapper flag such as --dblp-query, because the wrapper cannot pick key terms itself; the main call should then leave dblp out of --sources. Relay dblp(0) as "no record matched every term".
kept.recommendation: Adopt a spec change: remove the DBLP issue from the v3 Decisions table and from §3. In litsearch.py search, run DBLP as a separate `search.py "<2-3 key terms>" --sources dblp` call using a short form of the query, or have SKILL.md step 3 ask for a 2-to-3-term DBLP query each round. Relay `dblp(0)` as "no record matched every term", not as a failure.

kept.title: Re-vendor at HEAD (1666e69) and then wrap: HEAD fixes privacy and robustness gaps in our copy, but none of the wrapper's targets
kept.claim: Since a38b7b1, upstream has changed four of the nine scripts we ship (arxiv.py, common.py, search.py, snowball.py) in seven ways. (1) arXiv uses HTTPS. (2) arXiv answers go through common.http_xml, which parses only a body whose first markup is the Atom feed element, so no DTD or entity reaches the parser. It also caps nesting at 32, applies the 16 MiB body cap, classifies HTML, other XML and challenge pages, and retries through the shared _request loop. (3) Catch-all notes in search.py and snowball.py carry only the exception type. SourceError notes still carry a classified message, but arXiv's message no longer includes urllib's server reason phrase. (4) Snowball prints each distinct note once. (5) Both entry points print a `candidates: N (L lines, C characters on stdout)` stderr line, after the `sources:` line in search. (6) Snowball's default `--limit-per-seed` drops from 20 to 5, and the spec says to pass one seed per call. Our SKILL.md passes 20 explicitly, so the new default has no effect on our calls. (7) Both entry points force UTF-8 output. Nothing at HEAD changes the YAML emitter (titles with newlines still break), the exclusion, the compaction, or the 429 backoff policy for the JSON sources (RETRY_CODES and BACKOFF_SECONDS are the same). One thing does change for the wrapper: arXiv's 429 note now reads "arxiv: HTTP 429", where it used to read "HTTP Error 429: Too Many Requests", so the wrapper's `HTTP 429` trigger now matches arXiv. The wrapper is still needed, and re-vendoring and wrapping are complementary. A re-vendor touches nine headers, THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md, ATTRIBUTION.md, and the pinned hash in tests/test_experiment_proposal_plugin.py. That is a small cost.
kept.recommendation: Adopt: make re-vendoring all nine scripts at 1666e69 the first v3 task. That means new provenance headers and a new commit hash in OURS:plugins/experiment-proposal/THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md. Then write litsearch.py against HEAD's stderr contract. The `sources:` line is safe to parse, because upstream's spec requires it to stay byte-identical. The wrapper also has to handle the new `candidates:` line and notes that name only the exception type.

kept.title: Wrapper cannot attribute records to sources from captured stdout; consider importing the vendored modules in-process
kept.claim: The vendored scripts drop the source tag on output, so the YAML the wrapper captures cannot tie records to sources. For search, the sources: line on stderr already gives each source's returned count and shows which run each source returned records in. What it cannot give is which records came from which source, so the wrapper cannot count per-source records kept after exclude, or keep one source's records from its best run, without running one subprocess per source (--sources <name>). For snowball there is no --sources flag and no sources: line, so the wrapper gets no per-source information from a subprocess at all. The candidates: line exists only at HEAD; the pinned a38b7b1 scripts print no such line, so relaying it verbatim becomes a risk only after a re-vendor. Importing the modules in-process (federate, expand, enrich_bare_dois have the same signatures at pin and HEAD) does expose the source tag. But the counts then need the joined tags split, and they credit Crossref with records it only enriched. That route also needs the subprocess-stubbed test in spec line 85 rewritten.
kept.recommendation: Choose one of two designs in §3. (a) litsearch.py imports the vendored modules and calls `search.federate`, `snowball.expand` and `enrich_bare_dois` directly. That yields `_source` on every record, lets the wrapper retry one source alone, and lets it emit its own quoted YAML with no lenient parse; the vendored files stay untouched. (b) Keep subprocesses, run search once per source with `--sources <name>`, and report snowball as a single total. Either way, print a post-filter `candidates:` line of our own and do not relay upstream's.

kept.title: YAML emitter still unfixed at HEAD; the real break is a plain scalar with an interior newline, which the v3 lenient-parse rule misses
kept.claim: Upstream `_yaml_scalar` has not changed since commit ab58881, and our vendored copy (OURS skills/lit-search/scripts/common.py:498) is identical. It quotes a value only when the value is empty, contains a special character, starts with `-` or `?`, or has whitespace at either end. A title with embedded newlines and none of those triggers is therefore written unquoted across several lines. That is the only strict-parse failure in the six saved rounds, under both PyYAML 6.0.1 and pandoc 3.1.3 citeproc. Quoted abstracts whose continuation lines start at column 0 parse under both. The v3 spec diagnoses the cause correctly (line 10). Its output rule (line 68, quote every string) and the planned PR (line 73) would already fix the emitter, so adding `\n\r\t` to the trigger class is a narrower version of the same fix, not a correction. The real gap is the lenient-parse wording at line 67: it appends only lines "inside a quoted-string context", so it would not re-join the broken unquoted title. Upstream's test checks substrings, not a parse, so it cannot catch the bug.
kept.recommendation: Keep the upstream PR but narrow it to `_yaml_scalar`. Add `\n\r\t` to the trigger class and escape them in the quoted branch, or collapse whitespace runs in titles. Add a test that loads a title containing a newline with a real YAML parser. In the wrapper, change the lenient rule to: any line that does not start with `- id:` or an indented `key:` continues the previous scalar, quoted or not. Re-emit each string with `json.dumps(value, ensure_ascii=False)`, which is a valid YAML double-quoted scalar.

kept.title: Upstream already retries 429; the PR's backoff half duplicates it, and the wrapper should retry only the failing source
kept.claim:
At both the pin (a38b7b1) and HEAD, common._request retries HTTP 429 twice, waiting 3 s and then 6 s, and never reads Retry-After. Upstream states its intent in common.py:7 ("orchestrators degrade, never block") and in SKILL.md:58 ("the script backs off on 429 and degrades — no key setup is offered"). lit_live.py's "busy" label is a drift-detector classification only. A PR that "adds 429 backoff" therefore restates existing behaviour, and the spec's 20/40/80 s layer would add a longer block on top of it, against upstream's degrade-fast design.

In our run, kw2 finished 13 s after kw1, so its Semantic Scholar search came within 13 s of a successful one; the gap is between completion times, not start times. kw2 got a 429, as did every later keyword round, including kw4 and kw2b after a gap of about 16 minutes. Meanwhile the snowball rounds at 16:42:13 and 16:57:10 used Semantic Scholar's graph endpoints with no 429 at all. So the throttle hits the search endpoint specifically, and a 16-minute wait did not clear it. Nothing in the run shows that a 20/40/80 s retry would.

The v3 design reruns the whole search.py command. Each rerun sends one extra request each to Crossref, arXiv, OpenAlex and DBLP; arXiv's 3 s interval is tracked per process, so a fresh rerun does not sleep. If the wrapper retries at all, it should retry only Semantic Scholar via `--sources semantic_scholar`. Otherwise it should accept the degraded search and rely on snowball for Semantic Scholar coverage. The upstream PR should keep only the YAML quoting fix, or at most ask for Retry-After support. The cost is small: the change is spec-only, because litsearch.py does not exist yet.
kept.recommendation: Drop the 429 half of the PR, or reframe it as a small ask: honour `Retry-After` and make the retry ceiling configurable. In litsearch.py, retry only the source that returned 429 after 20, 40 and 80 s, using `search.py <q> --sources semantic_scholar` or an in-process call (lit-3), and keep Semantic Scholar searches at least 20 s apart across rounds.

kept.title: Exclude-by-DOI misses 15% of candidates; upstream matches on DOI, then normalized title
kept.claim: 84 of the 575 records across our six runs (14.6%) have no DOI, and 67 of the 361 in round 1. Many snowball records have no URL either. A DOI-only exclude file cannot hold these records at all, so any that a later round fetches again are shown again.
