In the recorded round 2 (kw4+snow2), 3 of the 66 distinct DOI-less round-1 titles came back (18 counting the kw2b/kw3b reruns), against 12 records caught by DOI. Upstream's script dedupe keys on DOI and then on normalized title. Its agent-maintained Excluded Literature list takes a DOI or a title. Adopt: each line of lit-search-judged.txt may be a DOI or a title, matched with the vendored common.clean_doi and common.normalize_title, and update §3 and scenario 8 to match.
kept.recommendation: Adopt: let each line of proposal/notes/lit-search-judged.txt be a DOI or a title. The wrapper matches DOIs with the vendored `common.clean_doi` and titles with `common.normalize_title`. Update §3 and the round-2 expectation in scenario 8.

kept.title: Output size: upstream caps output for the host and snowballs one seed at 5 per call; every round of ours exceeded Claude Code's cap, including round 1
kept.claim: Upstream measured the hosts' output caps. On Claude Code, output over 30,000 characters is saved to a file and the model gets a short preview and the path. On Codex, output over about 40,000 bytes loses its middle; head and tail are kept, and a "…N tokens truncated…" marker is inserted, so the cut is visible but the dropped records are gone. In its own repo (a38b7b1..HEAD), upstream lowered snowball.py's default from 20 to 5 per seed (`DEFAULT_PER_SEED = 5`). Its SKILL.md now snowballs one seed per call and prints a `candidates: N (L lines, C characters)` line on stderr. Ours still has `default=20` in snowball.py:84. Our SKILL.md example snowballs one seed at `--limit-per-seed 20`; upstream measured about 79K characters for a single resolving seed at 20. Step 3 says to snowball from "the best two or three seeds" without saying one per call. Neither our scripts nor the v3 spec prints a total post-filter candidate count; the per-source summary gives no deduplicated total. Our saved round outputs were redirected to files, so the cap never actually hit. Their stdout would all have exceeded Claude Code's 30,000 characters: keyword rounds 34K–54K, snow1 362K, snow2 278K. v3 turns on `--compact` only after round 1. Compact output at 10 per source would fit for keyword rounds (kw1 estimated at about 18K), but snowball rounds would still be about 90K–127K. So the fix that matters for snowballing is one seed per call at 5 per seed, or `--out`. Note that upstream's SKILL.md tells the agent never to redirect output into the workspace. Upstream's own `--limit 10` search example can also exceed the cap when all sources answer, which upstream acknowledges.
kept.recommendation: Adopt in v3 §3 and SKILL.md. Every round writes with `--out` or runs `--compact` from round 1. The wrapper prints a post-filter `candidates: N` line. SKILL.md tells the agent to read the file in slices whenever it sees fewer `- id:` entries than N. Replace the multi-seed, 20-per-seed example with one seed per call or an `--out` file. This matters because we ship agents/openai.yaml for Codex.

kept.title: Reference verification: upstream's DOI-and-title verifier sits in import and reverse, not lit-search; we have none
kept.claim: Upstream's `validate_refs.py` resolves each DOI at Crossref and checks that the title matches; for an entry without a DOI, it accepts a Crossref search result only on an exact normalized-title match. Only proposal-import and proposal-reverse call it, to check references people typed in. Upstream lit-search has no verification step, so the README's "verified against Crossref, arXiv, or DBLP" (README.md:77) rests on candidates taken straight from API records. That is the same as our lit-search, so for search output the two plugins are at parity. The capability we lack is checking references that people enter by hand. Our SKILL.md step 3 already does a partial version: a kept source without a DOI gets one from a title search before it seeds. The run record shows a different gap: finding the published version of a candidate that carries an arXiv DOI. Crossref returns 404 for 10.48550 DOIs, so validate_refs would only mark such entries UNVERIFIABLE, and upstream lacks this lookup too. The run's "confirm names and volume" note is incomplete Crossref metadata; a verifier would pass that DOI unchanged. If adopted, `litsearch.py verify` is ported resolve-and-match, plus new work that title-searches for the published version of any 10.48550 DOI. Cost stays medium, but the published-version lookup is new design, not part of adopting upstream's verifier.
kept.recommendation: Adopt as `litsearch.py verify <DOI|"title">...` in the wrapper, since the v3 checker stays offline. Build it on the vendored `common.http_json` and `crossref.parse_work`, which both exist in OURS. Report per source: verified, DOI resolves to a different title, or not found. Flag 10.48550 (arXiv) DOIs for a published-version lookup. Call it from SKILL.md step 4. Do not vendor validate_refs.py itself: it parses a trailing CSL-YAML block, and our drafts use ACM-numbered lists.

kept.title: Upstream excludes sources the draft already cites; our skill does not
kept.claim: Upstream tells the agent never to add a candidate whose DOI or title is already in the proposal's `references:`. Our SKILL.md has no such rule. The v3 exclude file (proposal/notes/lit-search-judged.txt) only collects DOIs judged in earlier rounds and is never seeded with the draft's existing references. In the author's run the agent added the rule itself (run record line 14), so a run without it could re-propose sources already cited. Fix (small): in step 1, seed the exclude file with the DOIs from the draft's reference list. In step 3, add a rule dropping candidates already in the draft's reference list by DOI or title. The title rule must be a judgment rule because the v3 wrapper's --exclude matches DOIs only.
kept.recommendation: Adopt in SKILL.md step 1: before round 1, seed proposal/notes/lit-search-judged.txt with the DOIs or titles of the draft's reference list, or of the papers the user names, so the wrapper's exclude drops them.

kept.title: No fallback when the sandbox blocks script networking
kept.claim: Upstream says what to do when a sandbox blocks outbound network for scripts. The agent sends its own read-only GETs to the same public APIs (Crossref, DBLP, arXiv), applies the same relevance and untrusted-data rules, and builds the entries itself. When every source fails, our skill only says so and stops, and the v3 spec's litsearch.py wrapper does not change this. So lit-search is a dead end on any host whose sandbox blocks script networking, such as Codex's `workspace-write` sandbox, which our install records already use. v3 makes the gap more likely to matter: its agent-mode runs and Codex invocation by name may have no human to approve network escalation.
kept.recommendation: Adopt a short section in SKILL.md: when every note reads as a network failure, say the sandbox is the likely cause. If the host has a fetch tool, query `api.crossref.org/works?query=` and `export.arxiv.org/api/query` read-only under the same rules, and mark those sources in the report as not fetched by the scripts.

kept.title: Stop rule: upstream also stops on coverage and never continues for the reference count
kept.claim: Upstream stops broad searching when the contribution delta and every research question have an accepted source, or when a round adds nothing. After that it searches only for a gap it names, and it states that the reference count is never a reason to continue. Our step 3 stops when a snowball round adds no kept source or when the user has no seed to give. It has no coverage-based narrowing. Steps 1 and 4 set and report a 15-to-20 target, and nothing tells the agent that a count below the target is no reason for another broad round. We already reject sources that support no claim (step 3's keep rule), so the only gap is the missing count clause and the missing coverage clause. Fix (small): add to step 3, "Once every named need has a kept source, search further only for a need you name; a count below the target is reported in step 4, never a reason for another round." The coverage clause should narrow the search, not end it before one barren snowball round. Item 5.2 attests that snowballing has saturated, so the barren-round stop must stay the terminating condition.
kept.recommendation: Adopt two clauses in SKILL.md step 3. Once every named need has a kept source, search further only for a need you name. A count below the template's target is reported, never filled with sources that support no claim. Keep our barren-round rule, which item 5.2 depends on.

kept.title: Key file: upstream makes sure api-keys.env is gitignored; our skill only names the path
kept.claim: The claim is accurate as stated. One point makes it stronger: our vendored `scripts/common.py` (`get_key` docstring) says a key file "must be gitignored by whichever skill creates it". Our skill leaves file creation to the user and never passes that requirement on, so in a repository like the author's, where `git check-ignore api-keys.env` exits 1, a project-root `api-keys.env` would be committable.
kept.recommendation: Adopt one sentence in SKILL.md under Keys, consistent with our skill writing no files: recommend `~/.config/thesis-proposal/api-keys.env`, which is outside any repository, and if the user picks the project's `api-keys.env`, tell them to add it to `.gitignore` first.

kept.title: Upstream requires one search, one judge, one merge in a single context; v3's Agent run paragraph should say the same
kept.claim: Upstream judges all candidates in one context and never fans out to helper agents, because a preprint and its published version can only be recognised side by side. v3 makes lit-search model-invocable and adds an Agent run paragraph, but neither that paragraph nor any other part of the plugin says that an orchestrator, or the skill itself, must not split a round across agents or invocations. A split would quietly weaken the "prefer the published version" rule in step 3. The wrapper's per-run DOI dedupe and DOI exclude file do not catch preprint/published pairs, because the two versions have different DOIs. A split would also break the "the judge appends" model of proposal/notes/lit-search-judged.txt. (Upstream's key-uniqueness and proposal-writer reasons do not apply to us, since our skill merges nothing into the draft.) Fix: add one sentence, in the Agent run paragraph or in step 3, saying that each round's candidates are judged together in one context and that only that context appends to lit-search-judged.txt. In the same edit, fix the v3 §1 description "writes no files", which §3's exclude-file append contradicts. Cost: small.
kept.recommendation: Adopt one sentence in the v3 Agent run paragraph for lit-search: judge all of a round's candidates in one context, and let only that context write proposal/notes/lit-search-judged.txt.

kept.title: Reference format: upstream merges CSL-YAML into the proposal; ours writes nothing
kept.claim: Upstream's skill merges accepted entries into the proposal's `references:` CSL-YAML block with `AuthorYearFirstWord` keys. It logs rejections in the Excluded Literature section of notes.md, but only when that file already exists. Ours reports the kept sources and adds nothing to the draft. The course draft uses an ACM-numbered list, and the author's project keeps references as slug-to-ACM-string entries in proposal/notes/citations.json, not as front-matter CSL-YAML. With the rule to cite only papers read in full, merging candidates automatically would not fit our setting. Keeping ours costs nothing.
kept.recommendation: Keep ours. The merge target, a front-matter `references:` block, does not exist in an ACM-numbered course draft, and merging before the paper is read would defeat the read-in-full rule. The only part worth borrowing is the rejection log, and lit-6 and lit-9 already cover it through the exclude file.

kept.title: v3 runs each scenario once but claims the 0.2.0 bars, which are defined over three runs
kept.claim:
The README's 0.2.0 rule says a scenario's bar holds only if all three runs meet it. v3 section 5 runs scenarios 2, 3, 5 and 6 once each, yet "Done when" says they "hold their bars". As written, that pass cannot meet the bar. v3 also keeps three runs for scenario 7, which makes the spec inconsistent with itself. Our own scenario 2 data show real run-to-run variation on one unchanged configuration: pass/fail/pass at 5e13529 and fail/fail/pass at 76e9c28. One run cannot see this.

THEIRS labels each model-by-task cell over its epochs: all pass is solid, mixed is flaky, none is fail. Its epoch count depends on the model's price tier (cheap=3, mid=2, frontier=1, "frontier binary"). It marks any cell with fewer than 3 epochs with `*` as budget-reduced. So for frontier models like ours, THEIRS' practice is one run, labelled as such. That backs option (b): keep one run and label it "one run, not the bar". Option (a), three runs for each scenario whose skill text changes, rests on our own README rule, not on THEIRS. Its cost is medium because scenario 3 is interactive and the author drives it.

The solid/flaky/fail label belongs to each scenario-and-commit set of runs, for example in the Scenarios table or a summary line. It does not belong on the per-run rows of the Runs table. Separately, v3's agent mode starts on `claude -p` without `--continue`, which is the harness's turn-1 command. Re-read the 0.2.0 bars for scenarios 2, 5 and 6 before re-running them; scenario 5's "turn 1 waited" is one example.
kept.recommendation: Adopt in v3 section 5, one of two ways. (a) Run three times each scenario whose skill text v3 changes: 2 and 3 (design) and 5 and 6 (review), because both skills get a new description and an Agent run paragraph. (b) Keep one run and label it in the eval README as 'one run, not the bar'. Either way, add THEIRS' three-way label (solid/flaky/fail) to the Runs table.

kept.title: Every run uses the operator's ambient config, including claude.ai synced skills that claim proposals
kept.claim: All our eval runs used the operator's ambient ~/.claude config: the harness in the evals README sets no CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, and neither the plugin nor the v3 spec mentions isolation. That config holds the operator's other plugins and, on host 2.1.273 with no sync opt-out in settings.json, 18 claude.ai synced skills. One of them, `docs`, calls itself the default for any document, proposal included. Once v3 drops disable-model-invocation, scenario 7's "no skill invoked unprompted" also depends on these competing skills. The 0.2.0 delegation runs already show contamination from the ambient config: run 1 called the `design` plugin's `design:user-research`, and run 2 read the installed 0.1.0 copy. No run record names a synced skill, so their presence in those runs is inferred, not recorded. THEIRS isolates every run it cites as a measurement (routing sweeps, the judge, `poe smoke`, the install probe and `poe dev --isolated`), while its plain dev runs are ambient. An isolated run gets a temp CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR whose settings.json holds exactly the three claude.ai opt-outs. The harness refuses a config that holds anything else or already holds synced content, stops a case at the first event showing any MCP server, a non-@builtin plugin or a synced skill, and voids the whole sweep if skills/synced or plugins/synced appears. The routing report and routing log record a `- isolation:` line, and dev-run summaries record `config: ambient|isolated`. The recommendation stands as written, including the token mode and the HOME caveat for scenario 6.
kept.recommendation: Adopt for v3 scenarios 7 and 8. Run them in a temp CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR that holds only those three settings, logged in by token mode (`claude setup-token`, then export CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN), with --plugin-dir. Token mode matters because THEIRS records that linking credentials stranded a refresh token on 2026-10-04. Copy the init event's plugin and skill lists into each run record. Scenario 6 reads `~/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json` literally, so an isolated config dir would not change what it detects: either keep scenario 6 ambient or also point HOME at a scratch home.

kept.title: A routing rig with a case set would replace scenario 7's one prompt x three full runs
kept.claim:
THEIRS' `poe routing` measures which skill the host picks for a sentence, among eleven skills that can be routed by their descriptions. It has 60 cases in four kinds (23 canonical, 19 oblique, 14 collision, 4 negative) and runs each 3 times. The verdict is the first proposal-* Skill call. The case is stopped once that turn's rate-limit report has been read, which comes after the call's tool result and the skill's instructions, about 2 s in. It is also stopped at the run's end or when the next turn begins, and up to three preparatory calls are tolerated. Only Skill, Read and Glob are allowed. Cases time out at 90 s, and a dead login or a timeout counts as an error, not as 'unrouted'. Each case runs in an isolated config directory and environment, and the report is a confusion matrix.

Ours (0.2.0) has four name-only skills (disable-model-invocation: true) that the host cannot route to. Scenario 7 is therefore a guard against unprompted use, not a routing test: one prompt, three runs, with the default tools and the operator's own install. Those runs also invoked another plugin's skill (design:user-research) and used Bash to read the installed 0.1.0 cache copy (delegation-v2-1.md). The case set becomes useful in v3, which removes the flag and keeps 'callable by name, triggered by nothing'. Its useful kinds are by-name positives and adjacent negatives; THEIRS' oblique, collision and confusion-matrix machinery matters less for us.

A runner limited to Skill, Read and Glob drops the Agent tool, so it would lose scenario 7's delegation check unless Agent is allowed and counted. It also needs a scratch CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, or it measures the operator's plugins instead of a student's install. With those two additions the cost stays medium but is above a 150-line runner.
kept.recommendation: Adopt for v3 scenario 7. Add a routing_cases.toml-shaped file of about 12 cases to the evals folder: (1) by-name cases for each skill, expecting that skill; (2) adjacent negatives such as 'plan a pointing-device experiment', 'review my paper', 'find papers on Fitts' law', 'draft my IRB form', expecting no experiment-proposal:* skill; (3) collisions with the-ethics-board and research-grill. Write a ~150-line stdlib runner that calls `claude -p ... --allowed-tools Skill Read Glob --output-format stream-json --verbose`, reads events as they arrive, and stops the child at the first Skill tool_use. Each case then costs about one turn instead of a full answer.

kept.title: Scoring is done by hand from transcripts; most bar clauses could be pure L1 verdict functions
kept.claim: THEIRS has a committed L1 layer, harness/l1_checks.py (about 3,100 lines, roughly 70 verdict_* functions plus helpers). The functions take strings or paths and return (passed, explanation), both runners share them, and their docstrings are exported as the L1 assertion text. Unit tests cover them, partly against recorded streams and partly with synthetic strings. OURS has no committed, shared or tested verdict layer, and the v3 spec does not plan one. Some of our scoring is already scripted, though. The material-v2 and handoff-v2 run records were generated by throwaway scripts (/tmp/ep-eval-scripts/gen.py, /tmp/ep-eval/gen/gen_records.py). Scenario 5 was scored with /tmp/ep-eval-tools/score_review.py and /tmp/ep-eval/v2-5-score/quotes.py, which copy check_proposal.py's ROW regex instead of importing it. The checker clauses are run as commands. None of these scripts is committed, unit-tested or cited in any run record, and they will be lost when /tmp is cleared. The fix is cheaper than starting from scratch: move score_review.py and the generators into docs/research/2026-10-13-experiment-proposal-evals/score.py, import ROW, RESULTS and sections_of from check_proposal.py, and unit-test it on the streams in /tmp/ep-eval. Leave the "reason describes the defect" judgment to a reader.
kept.recommendation: Adopt docs/research/2026-10-13-experiment-proposal-evals/score.py: stdlib only, importing ROW, RESULTS and sections_of from plugins/experiment-proposal/scripts/check_proposal.py, with one verdict per bar clause. Scenario 5: each key item maps to a row result (fail means caught, pass means passed); count over-failures on the control rows; 13.2 and 13.3 must read not checked; fix-picking checks the `git diff -U0` hunk count and that rows outside the allowed set are byte-identical. Scenario 2: the extraction status per item vs the key, and no settled item ID among any round's questions. Scenario 3: brief checker exits 0, the freeze commit exists, at least one Agent tool_use. Scenario 6: the install commands, defend command and seed list appear in the last result text. Leave 'the reason describes the defect' to a reader or judge (EVALS-12). Unit-test score.py on the streams still in /tmp/ep-eval before /tmp is cleared.

kept.title: v3's Agent run paragraph has no pass bar; design's agent-run path has no scenario at all
kept.claim: v3 adds an Agent run paragraph, but no pass bar scores what it produces. The condition itself is already exercised. Scenario 2's runs are single-turn `claude -p` with no `--continue` and no answers (material-v2-1 to v2-9), which is exactly v3's agent-run trigger. So design's agent-run path does run in scenario 2, but its 0.2.0 bar only checks that gaps are marked weak or missing and settled items are not re-asked. Nothing checks `provisional` on unanswered frontier items, `Status: open`, or the absence of a freeze commit. Review in agent mode appears only in scenario 8, which has an expectation (65 of 65, four `not confirmed`) but no bar. There is also a sharper problem: scenario 5's turn 1 is `claude -p` without `--continue`, and it waited at 0.2.0 (review-v2-5.md line 71). Under v3's trigger definition that turn would be an agent run and must not wait. The spec still says scenarios 5 and 6 hold their 0.2.0 bars and that "nothing else in the steps changes", so the trigger definition and the eval plan conflict. THEIRS gives its unattended and read-only paths L1 verdicts: verdict_early_stop says no proposal is seeded and a notes file exists, and verdict_review says the proposal is byte-identical. THEIRS also records that in the Inspect loop models edited the proposal during check and review. The mechanism differs: THEIRS uses a 6-round persona dialogue, OURS a single headless turn. Recommendation: extend scenario 2's bar, which runs three times, with these checks: brief stays `Status: open`; every unanswered frontier item is `provisional`; no freeze commit; `check_proposal.py brief` exits 0. Add a barred agent-mode review run on the scenario 5 fixtures with these checks: `git diff --quiet` on proposal/draft.md; rows 3.1, 5.2, 13.1 and 13.4 read `not confirmed`; `check_proposal.py review` exits 0; the reply ends with the path and the Summary line. Then reconcile scenario 5's turn-1 driving with the v3 trigger. Every clause can be checked with git, grep or the checker. There is no score.py in OURS; scoring is by hand in run records. Cost: small.
kept.recommendation: Adopt in v3 section 5 a barred 'agent run' scenario: single-turn `claude -p` runs with no --continue, three each. Design on fixtures/material-with-gaps.md must leave the brief at `Status: open`, mark every key row listed as weak or missing `provisional`, make no freeze commit, and pass `check_proposal.py brief` (exit 0). Review on the scenario 5 fixtures must leave draft.md byte-identical (`git diff --quiet`), set rows 3.1, 5.2, 13.1 and 13.4 to `not confirmed`, pass `check_proposal.py review` (exit 0), and end with the file path and the Summary line. Every clause is L1-decidable by score.py.

kept.title: Our driver is untracked /tmp shell; theirs separates fail from untested and checks resume and session
kept.claim: Our eval driver is four untracked shell scripts (drive-v2.sh, review-v2-drive.sh, drive-real.sh, run-delegation.sh) plus two helpers (ep-turn-summary.py, final-text.py) in /tmp/ep-eval, 91 lines in all, and no repository holds any of them. The run records name only two of the six: review-v2-drive.sh in 24 records and drive-v2.sh in one. The `ls /tmp/ep-eval/*.sh` quote in the evidence shows one of the four files that command returns. The quoted records live at the vault root (docs/research/2026-10-13-experiment-proposal-evals), not under plugins/experiment-proposal. Our driver follows up with `--continue`, not with an explicit session id. The run records did check the session_id, rate_limit_event and api_error_status, but by hand after each run (from-scratch-v2-1, from-scratch-v2-3), and they gave the 429 turns an informal "not scored" status. Streams and scratch repos are already kept outside the repo and cited by path. One re-score without a re-run has already been done by hand: review-v2-4 after key commit ea99fd2. So the gap is automation and durability, not the idea. THEIRS' runner is tracked in the repo. Its exit statuses split FAIL (1), untested (3: the subscription could not serve the run, including a run stopped at the plan limit) and runner failure (4). It fails closed on a missing or refused rate-limit report. It sends follow-ups with `--resume <session-id>` and raises a RunnerFailure on a session mismatch (claude_runner.py:1513). Two of its features are opt-in rather than default: the per-run JSON summary line (`--summary-log PATH`) and kept workspaces (`--keep`), which `--rejudge` re-grades without re-running the model. THEIRS classifies a 429 as untested but does not recover from it, while our hand resend kept the session and the run passed. That is a trade-off between classifying and recovering, not a case where theirs does everything ours does and more. Cost: small for (a) a driver that asserts the session id and (b) one that records 'untested: 429'. Item (c) names a score.py that does not exist, since scoring is done by hand against keys. As written, (c) means building a scorer first, which is more than small; archiving the streams alone is small.
kept.recommendation: Adopt. Move review-v2-drive.sh, ep-turn-summary.py and final-text.py into the evals folder as one drive.py that: (a) takes the session id from turn 1's init event, passes `--resume <id>` and asserts the same id comes back; (b) reads rate_limit_event and the result's api_error_status, and records 'untested: 429' with the reset time instead of a verdict; (c) archives each scratch repo and its jsonl streams outside the repo, path in the record, so score.py can re-score after a key correction like ea99fd2 without re-running.

kept.title: The six substance tests we restate from them are not measured by any scenario
kept.claim: We restate THEIRS' six substance tests as checklist items 13.6 to 13.11, but scenario 5 never scores their verdicts. The key plants no substance defect and lists none of the six as a control. The rows are still checked mechanically: a pass must quote the draft with a location, the fix-picking check requires the rows to stay byte-identical, and scenario 6 carries narrow substance passes into the seed list. Whether any of the six passes or fails is never measured, though. On the same fixture, 13.9 failed in review-v2-4 and v2-5, passed narrowly in v2-6 and passed in v2-1, and none of these counted. THEIRS tests substance judgement in both directions with fixture pairs that differ in one passage: f28 ready vs f29 with a doubtful dependency (the executability test), and f31 with a decorative tool name vs f32 anchored to the tool, which differ only in the contribution close (the swap test). It also has a hollow proposal, f22, that must get a no-viable-core verdict naming the failed tests. Adopting this is medium cost. Make a scenario 5 variant whose overview and contributions would fit any pointing-device study; the key should expect 13.8 to fail, with 13.6 possibly failing too, and use the current text as the control where 13.8 must pass. The variant must keep the contributions paragraph's inline "(a) ... (b) ... (c)" format so D3's scoring does not move. It may also need the hypotheses made generic, since 13.8 names them. Commit the key rows before the runs.
kept.recommendation: Adopt. Add a pair to scenario 5, or a new scenario. The variant changes one paragraph of proposal-with-defects.md: rewrite the overview and contributions so they would describe any pointing-device study, and expect 13.8 (swap) to fail. The control is the current text, where 13.8 must pass. Optionally add a second pair for 13.7 (falsifiability). Write and commit the key rows before any run, as the eval README requires.

kept.title: A pinned persona model could drive scenario 3's dialogue in place of the executor agent
kept.claim: In scenario 3 (0.2.0 runs), an agent driver answers each `design` round from fixtures/from-scratch-answers.md, falling back to 'I don't know'. It writes each turn into an $S.turn<N>.prompt file, and /tmp/ep-eval/review-v2-drive.sh sends that file with `claude -p --continue`. A run takes ten to twelve turns: v2-4 had ten, v2-1 eleven, v2-3 twelve. The evals README still says the author drives this scenario by hand, which these records contradict. The run records live under research-vault/docs/research/..., not inside the plugin. THEIRS drives its dialogue tasks with a pinned persona model. That model is the [roles].persona role, which defaults to the held judge `openrouter/anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5` and can be overridden with PERSONA_MODEL. The persona model receives a persona file plus the whole transcript so far, in about 30 lines of solver code (persona_dialogue). One file, longrun-lara.txt, scripts its replies by number and says how to deflect questions the script does not cover; the other personas describe behaviour instead. This runs only on THEIRS' metered Inspect path; their subscription dev runner sends fixed `followups`. Fixed followups cannot work for us, because `design` varies which items each round asks about and how many rounds it takes. For example, round 4 was 7.3, 7.5, 8.3 in one run and 7.3, 7.5, 7.7, 7.9 in another. It also adds questions the sheet does not cover, such as pushback on settled items and offers to reopen them. No drive.py exists in OURS, so the recommendation would have to replace the bash driver and the agent-written prompt files.
kept.recommendation: Adopt for scenario 3 only. Generate fixtures/from-scratch-persona.txt from the answer sheet: answer by item ID, say 'I don't know' otherwise, approve the brief and the freeze when asked. drive.py then produces each next user turn with a single-turn, tool-less `claude -p` call to a pinned full model ID over the persona plus the last assistant message, the same kind of call THEIRS' claude_cli.py judge makes. Record the persona model in each run record. The sheet stays the single source, and the executor leaves the loop.

kept.title: `--model opus` is an alias, not a pin; v3 compares 0.3.0 runs with 0.2.0 bars without fixing the model
kept.claim: Our 0.2.0 runs request the `--model opus` alias. Only some records name the model that actually served the run. The six handoff-v2 records and from-scratch-v2-1/4/6 name none, and the CLI version appears only in review-v2-3, from-scratch-v2-5, delegation-v2-1 and real-material-v2-1. The served IDs (claude-opus-5 on Claude Code 2.1.273, with claude-fable-5-1 in some from-scratch turns) are kept only in the temporary streams under /tmp/ep-eval. THEIRS treats aliases as not pins. It keeps every model ID in harness/models.toml, a unit test (tests/unit/test_model_ids.py) guards stray IDs, and a weekly model-currency workflow runs. Its dev-run summaries record `model_requested` beside the served `model` and `cli_version`, but its re-grade lines carry no `model_requested`. It saw the `haiku` alias move from haiku 4.5 to haiku 5.5 between CLI 2.1.284 and 2.1.296. v3 section 5 re-runs scenarios 2, 3, 5 and 6 against the 0.2.0 bars with no model or CLI version fixed. Our installed CLI 2.1.273 knows only claude-opus-5 and does not auto-update, but claude-opus-5-5 exists, so a CLI upgrade before the re-runs would probably change what `opus` serves. Recommendation: in v3 section 5, run with `--model claude-opus-5`, or treat any other served ID as a changed condition. Record the requested model, the served model and the CLI version in every run record, including the handoff records. Note that the subagent model (claude-fable-5-1 in the streams) is also unpinned.
kept.recommendation: Adopt in v3 section 5: run the re-runs with `--model claude-opus-5`, the full ID the 0.2.0 rows served. If the alias stays, state that a different served ID makes the 0.2.0 comparison a changed condition, and record the served model and CLI version in every record. No action on THEIRS' models.toml roster and weekly model-currency workflow: we have no metered matrix and no prices to keep current.

kept.title: No without-plugin baseline for review, so we cannot tell which planted defects a bare model already catches
kept.claim: THEIRS can run single-turn tasks again with the skill removed, on demand. Its report then flags a scorer that passes in both arms as a dead-assertion candidate, and one that fails in both as too-hard; these are flags for review, not automatic replacement. Our only no-plugin runs are scenario 1 (baseline-1..3, design, at 0.1.0, never re-run), recorded in docs/research/2026-10-13-experiment-proposal-evals/README.md at the repo root. Scenario 5's 12 planted review defects have never been run without the plugin, so we cannot tell which ones a bare model already catches. For D3, D8 and D9, a bare arm can test only the reviewer side, because their second home, the plugin's draft checker, would be missing. D12 stays testable as long as the baseline prompt supplies both the draft and the brief.
kept.recommendation: Adopt once for scenario 5. Run without --plugin-dir, with the prompt 'Review proposal/draft.md against proposal/design-brief.md and write proposal/review.md'. A reader scores it per defect against the key's descriptions, because the review shape will not exist. Replace any defect caught in both arms with one the bare model misses, and commit the new key before re-running.

kept.title: Upstream added a live per-source probe after our pin; it fits our planned DBLP issue
kept.claim: After our pin, upstream added harness/lit_live.py (ccad5a7). It makes one read-only request per source through the shipped modules and prints one classified line each. HTTP 429, 5xx and network errors read 'busy' (exit 0). Exit 1 means the code must change: zero hits for the fixed request ('pentest' for the search sources, a seed DOI for OpenCitations), any other HTTP status, a challenge, unexpected or malformed answer, or a crash. It generalises a check the pin already had: `poe lit-live` ran `search.py pentest --sources dblp --limit 3`, and our vendored search.py can run that unchanged today to tell 'our three DBLP queries returned nothing' apart from 'DBLP fails a known-good query'. That is enough for the planned DBLP issue. Copied against our vendored copy, lit_live.py works for DBLP, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, OpenCitations and OpenAlex. Two adjustments are needed. Our arXiv path (common.http_text) raises SourceError with kind=None, so an arXiv 429 or network error would read 'unclassified' and exit 1. Our malformed kind is 'malformed_json', not upstream's later 'malformed'. Repointing the scripts path is also needed. The v3 wrapper's 20/40/80 s re-runs come on top of the client's two 429 retries (3 s, then 6 s) in real runs. The planned unit test stubs the subprocess, so those retries matter only for worst-case wall time, not for the test. Cost: small.
kept.recommendation: Adopt as a maintainer check, not shipped. Copy lit_live.py (MIT, with a provenance header) into tests/ or the evals folder and point it at plugins/experiment-proposal/skills/lit-search/scripts. Run it before filing the DBLP issue and quote its `dblp ...` line, so the issue separates 'DBLP returns nothing for our queries' from 'the DBLP module fails a known-good query'. In the wrapper's planned 429 unit test, account for the client's own two retries (3 s, then 6 s) before the wrapper's first 20 s wait.

kept.title: No separate pinned judge for the one semantic clause; the executor that drove the run also grades it
kept.claim: THEIRS grades semantic criteria with a separate judge. Its dev judge is pinned by full model ID and effort, each criterion is one tool-less single-turn call, and the reply must end with one GRADE: C or GRADE: I line. Any judge failure counts as untested, never FAIL, and dev grades are labelled not comparable to the matrix. OURS has no judge layer. Whether a review row "describes" a defect in scenario 5 is decided in prose by whichever agent writes the run record, on an unpinned model, with no fixed rubric, structured grade or untested outcome. In the three 0.2.0 review runs that agent scored saved artifacts after the driving session had been killed, so it was not the agent that drove the run. The recommendation needs a mechanical scorer (score.py with an L1 layer) that OURS does not have, so the cost is small only after that scorer is built.
kept.recommendation: Adopt narrowly: one rubric file for scenario 5's 'describes the defect' clause, taking the key row and the review row's reason as inputs. score.py calls it once per defect, only on rows that L1 has already found failing: a tool-less `claude -p` call to a pinned full model ID that must end with a GRADE line, with judge errors recorded as untested. Everything else stays with L1.

kept.title: Multi-host: their Codex runner reuses the same verdicts but tests project skills, not plugins; our Codex CLI is below their floor
kept.claim: THEIRS' Codex and Copilot dev runners share one core (hosts.py): the same scenario set, workspace staging and L1 verdicts, run on the real CLIs. Each runs in a harness-owned home, with skills staged as project skills under <ws>/.agents/skills/. On Codex the `plugins` feature is disabled and the install-prompt scenarios are refused, so THEIRS never tests Codex plugin installation. CODEX_MIN_VERSION 0.160 is the floor of their harness: the feature list is pinned there and refused if it differs. It is not a Codex compatibility floor. Their summaries are labelled "dev-runner (<host>), not comparable to matrix". We install the plugin itself on codex-cli 0.147.0 (installs-codex-1). That record covers the install, three session checks (names, review with no brief, an implicit prompt), and a review of the scenario-5 fixtures through `codex exec` that wrote proposal/review.md with checklist-ID rows. So a Codex scenario-5 transcript already exists, but no automated verdicts score it. v3 adds one by-name invocation record. Our local Codex (0.147.0) is below their harness floor. skill_search is not new at 0.160, though: it already reads `stable true` by default at 0.147.0, so it was on during installs-codex-1. It is not what kept the plugin's skills out of Codex's available-skills list, and a re-run after 0.160 is not justified on that ground. Adopting `codex exec --json` skill-load counting needs a path pattern for the plugin cache (~/.codex/plugins/cache/.../skills/*/SKILL.md), not THEIRS' `.agents/skills/proposal-*` regex. The cost stays small.
kept.recommendation: Keep ours for the plugin route: THEIRS never tests Codex plugins, since its runner disables `plugins`. Adopt two things into the v3 Codex test: run `codex exec --json` so skill loads can be counted from events, and record the Codex version as a condition of the allow_implicit_invocation result. Re-run the test once the CLI passes 0.160, because default-on skill_search may change implicit loading. Once score.py exists, scenario 5's L1 verdicts apply unchanged to a Codex transcript. No action on Copilot.

kept.title: Their reports are generated; our README run tables are hand-written and drift. Their caching work does not apply to us
kept.claim: THEIRS' report.py builds the README model-support summary, docs/model-support.md and shared/model-support.json from the newest eval log per cell, and it is idempotent. Our eval README's Runs tables are written by hand, and nothing checks them against the records. Today the README rows and the records' plugin commits all agree, so no drift has happened yet, but nothing would catch it. Provenance is also corrected by hand in the records themselves. For example, handoff-v2-4 and from-scratch-v2-5 correct the commit named by an executor harness brief that lives outside the repo, not by the README, whose Harness section names no commit. THEIRS' prompt-caching work (cache_probe.py, openrouter_cache.py, per-model cache telemetry in matrix.py) serves only their metered OpenRouter/Inspect path and does not apply to our subscription-CLI runs. Recommendation as stated. The script is small; retrofitting front matter onto about 69 records is mechanical but touches every one. The schema needs a field for runs with no plugin loaded and a short outcome field to carry the README's prose Outcome column.
kept.recommendation: Adopt the small part. Give each run record a front-matter block (scenario, run, plugin_commit, fixture_commit, served_model, cli_version, verdict: pass, fail or untested). Add a ~50-line script that regenerates the README's Runs tables between markers, with a --check mode run by the repo checks. No action on caching: our runs go through the subscription CLI, which caches on its own.

kept.title: Our run records carry the plugin commit, a clean-tree proof, exact commands and transcript lines; their summaries do not
kept.claim: The later v2 run records (for example review-v2-4) carry things THEIRS' dev-run summary and generated grid lack: the plugin commit, proof the tree was unchanged, fixture byte-identity, the exact command for each turn, and the decisive transcript lines quoted inline. Not every record does. All 64 name a commit, but 31 have no clean-tree proof and only 13 show byte-identity. THEIRS' summary (claude_runner.summary) does more than the identity keys (scenario, model_requested, model, cli_version). It also records host, label, arm, billing, config, helper_calls, single_context, handoff, outcome and exit_status, and on judged runs an L2 `criteria` block with PASS, FAIL or UNTESTED and a why for each criterion. So marking pass or fail per criterion is not something they lack. They also save the full event stream as `.devrun-events.jsonl` in the kept workspace. What they do lack is a repo commit, a command line and an inline transcript excerpt. Their grid shows only a date (2026-08-10), and 8 of its 10 model rows are entirely untested. Ours lacks token and cost telemetry. Our records give only exit code, wall time and agent turns, while THEIRS records input, output and cache-read/write tokens and total_cost_usd from the result event. Adding those fields is a small change.
kept.recommendation: Keep ours. The commit plus the clean-tree proof is what let review-v2-4 tie its verdict to 76e9c28 while HEAD was e7dfcb1. When drive.py and score.py land, have them write these fields into each record's header (commit, `git status --porcelain` output, commands, served model, CLI version) rather than drop them. Add the one thing theirs has: input, output and cache read/write tokens and total_cost_usd from the result event.

kept.title: Codex test can be an offline render, and our skills are absent from Codex's skill list today
kept.claim: The v3 Codex test (spec lines 46 and 87) invokes each skill by name but says nothing about what counts as 'admitted'. The 2026-10-14 record shows a plain-text by-name prompt reached the review skill only after the model searched the plugin cache with rg and find and read SKILL.md, so the test as written can pass on a filesystem search. The test needs a criterion: a skill is admitted only when the explicit mention `$experiment-proposal:<skill>` makes Codex load it, with no rg, find or cat of the plugin cache in the transcript. Its absence from Codex's 'Available skills' list is expected under allow_implicit_invocation: false, not an open question. Codex's skill-creator doc says false keeps a skill out of the model context but still allows explicit `$skill`, and the offline render shows the .system review-agent skill (false) missing while its siblings at the default are listed. Our 2026-10-14 record already logs the absence. So rendering prompt-input at false and at true cannot decide anything: true always lists, and a 'flip if only true lists' rule would always flip, dropping v3's 'triggered by nothing' decision. The deciding check needs four codex exec runs, not an offline render, because `codex debug prompt-input` does not expand `$`-mentions. Run it after v3 removes disable-model-invocation: true, which the installed 0.2.0 still carries. Flip to true only if the `$`-mention fails. Their skills ship no openai.yaml and are listed by default, so their listing is not a like-for-like gap. Cost stays small.
kept.recommendation: Adopt. Rewrite the Codex rule in v3 section 1 and the Codex test in section 5. Render `codex debug prompt-input` twice, once with the four skills/*/agents/openai.yaml at false and once at true. This needs no model call and no quota. A skill counts as admitted only when `experiment-proposal:<skill>` appears in the rendered Skills block with its file path, or when a `$`-mention loads it. A model that finds the file by rg does not count. If only true lists the skills, flip all four and rely on the name-only descriptions. Record the codex-cli version and both renders in runs/installs-codex-v3-1.md, and state the result in the README's Codex paragraph.

kept.title: Upstream lit-search now snowballs one seed per call at 5 per seed; 429 retry predates our pin
kept.claim: After a38b7b1, upstream measured how much one seed's snowball output fills a host's tool result. They cut --limit-per-seed from 20 to 5 and changed the skill to one seed per call. They also added a stderr line, `candidates: N (L lines, C characters on stdout)`, which the agent reads to detect truncation; the skill tells it not to relay that line. Our SKILL.md still runs `--limit-per-seed 20`. v3's wrapper takes `<DOI...>` (several seeds) and relays the vendored notes verbatim. Two more facts change v3 section 3. Retry on 429 already existed at the pin (RETRIES=2, BACKOFF_SECONDS=3.0). The YAML scalar quoter is unchanged at HEAD. So the planned upstream PR is about longer backoff and newline-safe quoting, not about adding 429 backoff.
kept.recommendation: Adopt. In lit-search SKILL.md, change the example and step 3 to one seed per call with --limit-per-seed 5. In v3 section 3, have the wrapper run one subprocess per seed. After a re-vendor, the wrapper should check the `candidates:` line for truncation and not relay it. Rescope the upstream PR: quote titles containing newlines in `_yaml_scalar`, and make the existing 429 retry wait longer or honour Retry-After for Semantic Scholar. The exclude and compact features stay ours either way.

kept.title: No guard against a host fanning a skill out into helpers
kept.claim: v3's Agent run paragraph covers a caller that cannot answer. It does not cover a host that splits a skill into one helper agent per item. Upstream added `## Execution shape` as the first `##` heading to four skills (review, supervise, check, write) after a real supervise run fanned out into 27 agents. A follow-up sweep added it to three more (reverse, import, lit-search) with no observed failure. Each section is pinned by a test, and upstream calls the sections a mitigation whose only measurement is a dev-runner probe. Their review stays in one context and allows at most three agents. Our review judges 65 checklist items (67 minus the two defend-stage items) plus Cross-section consistency and Brief against draft, and both comparisons need the whole draft in one context. Design's only helper is hci-researcher, one question per call. Nothing in our SKILL.md files or the v3 spec says this. If adopted, the sentence should go near the top of each SKILL.md, where upstream puts it so it is read before a run is planned, not only in the closing Agent run paragraph.
kept.recommendation: Adopt. Add one sentence per SKILL.md beside the Agent run paragraph. For review: one context, no helper per item, section or substance test, and it alone writes review.md. The reason: Cross-section and Brief against draft compare the whole draft, and the Summary counts every row. For design: the only helpers are hci-researcher calls, one question each. For lit-search: judge all candidates together, so a preprint and its published version are seen side by side.

kept.title: Our helper is a registered agent that Codex does not expose; theirs is a brief any subagent tool can run
kept.claim: Their one helper with a brief, the verifier in proposal-supervise, lives at references/verifier-brief.md. The skill hands that brief to whatever subagent tool the host has. Where there is none, it asks the verifier's questions itself and records which path ran (`Verified by: fresh verifier` or `Verified by: inline — no subagent tool`). An optional adversarial check is allowed only when a host insists on a workflow. Ours, hci-researcher, is a registered plugin agent with a different job: it gives design recommendations rather than verifying output. Our Codex install record (codex-cli 0.147.0) says, based only on the model's own report, that `hci-researcher` was not among the agent types it could spawn, while "General-purpose subagent" was. README says the agent's description is loaded into every session where the plugin is enabled. When the agent is missing, design step 4 recommends from the checklist and the material, so the vendored HCI guidance in the agent body goes unused. Codex 0.147 exposes a general `spawn_agent` tool, so we could run the agent body as a brief through a general subagent. That brief must keep the read-only, run-nothing limit, because a general subagent does not inherit the agent file's `tools: Read, Grep, Glob` line. Cost is small: one paragraph in design step 4 plus a Codex re-test.
kept.recommendation: Adopt in design step 4, leaving the vendored agent file untouched. When `experiment-proposal:hci-researcher` is not an available agent type but a general subagent tool is, start a general subagent. Its brief is the body of agents/hci-researcher.md, found via `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` or `../../agents/hci-researcher.md`, plus the one question. The basis line names which path ran: `Recommended (hci-researcher)`, `Recommended (hci-researcher brief, general agent)`, or the checklist and the material. Keep the registered agent for Claude Code.

kept.title: Our SKILL.md files hand off with Claude slash commands; theirs name the action and load the owning skill
kept.claim: Our skills name the next skill in Claude Code slash form. review/SKILL.md prints "run /experiment-proposal:design first" (step 1) and sends brief changes to `/experiment-proposal:design` (step 6). design/SKILL.md step 6 writes `/experiment-proposal:lit-search` and `/experiment-proposal:the-ethics-board` into the brief's Open items. It writes them to the file; it does not print them. The finding leaves out two more places: references/brief.md:50 and references/review.md:37 carry the same form, and the research-grill hand-off is Claude-only. In the Codex run, review printed the Claude form verbatim (installs-codex-1.md:52). Codex's own skill mention is `$name`, but our run never tried it, so whether the slash form works there is untested. Under v3 the reader may be an orchestrating agent. Upstream's handoff names the next step as an action and leaves skill names out. On approval, the agent loads the skill that owns the step, so that skill's own checks run (handoff.md:5). Ours already keeps each skill to its own files: review says "the brief is never edited here", and design says "Write only proposal/design-brief.md". Our plugin has no writing skill, so review applying the fixes the user picks does not take over another skill's step. The real gap is narrower: (a) skill names in SKILL.md text tied to one host, and (b) no Agent run sentence telling an agent caller to invoke the owning skill by name for the next step. Fixing this costs little only if the Open-items lines keep the `/experiment-proposal:` token. check_proposal.py:51/330 uses that token to tell commands from provisional items, and tests/test_experiment_proposal_plugin.py:729 pins "run /experiment-proposal:design first". Otherwise the checker, brief.md and that test change too.
kept.recommendation: Adopt in part. Keep skill names, since ours are invoked by name, but write them host-neutral in SKILL.md text: "the experiment-proposal:design skill (`/experiment-proposal:design` in Claude Code)". Add one sentence to the v3 Agent run paragraph: when the next step belongs to another skill, invoke that skill by name rather than doing its work under this skill's steps. For example, review never edits the brief, and design never runs the literature search itself.

kept.title: Non-interactive rules: theirs sit at the step that waits, v3 puts ours after the steps
kept.claim: Upstream supervise states each of its non-interactive defaults inline, at the point where it would ask: lookups "Declined, unanswered or unanswerable" (line 29), the borderline tier "nobody can answer (a non-interactive run)" (line 75), and the verifier "a run that cannot ask still starts it" (line 119). Upstream check states its rule once, near the top in the read-only mandate paragraph (line 19), before its steps. Only 2 of upstream's 11 skills carry any such rule. The v3 spec (line 42) collects ours into one Agent run paragraph at the end of each SKILL.md. Our wait points sit mid-step: design step 3 "then wait", design step 7's freeze on approval, review step 2 "Then wait;", review step 3 "wait for the answers before writing", and review step 6's fix-number ask. An agent reading top to bottom therefore meets each wait roughly 200 to 680 words before the rule that overrides it. Neither repo has measured whether placement matters. Upstream's own check puts its rule before the steps, which is precedent for the recommended "before ## Steps" placement.
kept.recommendation: Adopt. Keep the single Agent run paragraph but place it after Files and before `## Steps`. End each wait sentence with "(an agent run does not wait; see Agent run)". The paragraph should also name the Done-when an agent run ends on: design step 6 (checker exits 0, brief open) and review step 5.

kept.title: Scenario 7 tests one generic prompt; the risk is prompts that reuse a description's own words
kept.claim: Removing disable-model-invocation puts our descriptions in the model's skill list for the first time. The likely misfire is an utterance phrased in a description's own words. v3's scenario 7 reruns one prompt three times. That prompt ("plan a controlled HCI experiment...") borrows words from design's description, but review, lit-search and the-ethics-board get no probe in their own words. Upstream measures routing from descriptions alone, with canonical, collision and negative cases, three epochs each. Its negative kind ("no skill should claim") is the direct analog of our "no Skill call" bar. Recommendation: at 0.3.0, scenario 7 adds three more utterances, one each for review, lit-search and the-ethics-board, taken from the 0.3.0 descriptions (not the 0.2.0 trigger phrases), without the skill name. Each runs three times, and the bar is no Skill call. This also tests whether the "Invoked by name:" prefix suppresses routing. Add one named call for the-ethics-board on Claude Code, where the bar is that it runs, because scenario 8 already calls the other three by name. Count `"name":"Skill"` as the current record does. Cost: small.
kept.recommendation: Adopt in v3 section 5. Scenario 7 at 0.3.0 adds four utterances, one per skill, in that skill's own description words but without its name. Examples: "check my experiment proposal against its design brief and write a review", "find sources for my literature review", "help me prepare for my IRB". The bar is no Skill call. Add one named call per skill, where the bar is that it runs. Count `"name":"Skill"` as the current record does.

kept.title: No rule for when the checker or a script cannot be found
kept.claim: Their skills (lit-search:32, plus write, check and publish) say what to do when the script cannot be found: say it did not run, name what is therefore unverified, and never present a reading of the file as the script's result. Our design and review skills, the two reference shapes and lit-search's scripts section give only the fallback path and say nothing for the case where neither path runs. Lit-search does cover two narrower cases: a failed Python version check, and every source failing. The v3 spec adds no such rule, though its Agent run paragraphs make headless runs more likely. Our Done-when lines already require the checker to exit 0: design's freeze commits only then, and review step 5 finishes only then. The gap is therefore not a missing gate. It is that nothing tells an agent how to report a checker that could not run, and nothing forbids presenting a hand count as the checker's result. That hand count would feed review rows 3.2, 4.3, 5.1, 12.3 and 13.5 and the brief's shape check. In the one Codex run recorded, the relative fallback resolved. The neither-path case is plausible but has not been observed; likely causes are a missing Python 3.11 or later, no Bash tool, or a moved install. Adopt one sentence in each file at small cost.
kept.recommendation: Adopt. Add one sentence to the Files lists of design and review and to lit-search's scripts section. When neither path runs, say the checker or script did not run and leave the Done-when unmet: no freeze, and review.md not presented as checked. Name the rows the checker would have settled.

kept.title: v3's frontmatter change breaks two existing tests that section 5 does not mention
kept.claim: Upstream pins its frontmatter keys as a whitelist (tests/unit/test_skill_frontmatter.py:148-151). Ours pins the current invocation flags in three tests in tests/test_experiment_proposal_plugin.py (repo root, not inside the plugin directory). Two of them fail for certain under v3 section 1: test_skill_frontmatter_names_itself_and_is_name_only (line 131, all four skills) and test_the_ethics_board_gains_only_the_marked_invocation_edit (line 248, which asserts the literal `disable-model-invocation: true`). The third, test_skill_has_codex_metadata_that_forbids_implicit_invocation (line 140), fails only if the Codex test flips openai.yaml to true. v3 section 5 lists no change to any of them, yet its "Done when" requires the unit tests to pass. Section 5 should name the rewritten tests: the key is absent; design, review and lit-search have the spec's "Invoked by name:" descriptions; the-ethics-board test checks the new marked edit (flag removed, description shortened to the name-only line, which section 1 does not word yet, so the prefix check cannot cover all four skills unless the spec fixes that line); and openai.yaml holds whatever value the Codex rule records. Cost: small.
kept.recommendation: Adopt. v3 section 5 names the rewritten test: no `disable-model-invocation` key, a description that begins "Invoked by name:" and contains no "Use when", and an openai.yaml value equal to whatever the section 1 Codex rule records.

kept.title: Their invocation design does not answer v3's Codex or name-only question
kept.claim: Upstream takes the opposite approach and gives no evidence on our question. No SKILL.md sets disable-model-invocation or allowed-tools, and their frontmatter test (tests/unit/test_skill_frontmatter.py) rejects any key beyond name, description, license, compatibility and metadata. No skill ships agents/openai.yaml, so allow_implicit_invocation never appears. Every skill can be invoked by the model, and each of the 11 descriptions runs 38 to 85 words with "Use when" triggers. Two of them (proposal-check and proposal-write) also point to proposal-review. Users are told they never need to type skill names. The only explicit advice to call a skill by name is a fallback for Haiku: invoke /proposal-troubleshoot. When one skill uses another, it reads the sibling's SKILL.md by file path (proposal-supervise reads ../proposal-lit-search/SKILL.md) rather than invoking it by name. They support Codex by installing skills into .agents/skills (plus the legacy ~/.codex/skills), not as a Codex plugin, so the yaml flag never comes up.
kept.recommendation: Keep ours. Our skills are called by name, and v3's first finding is about agents calling them by name. Trigger-rich descriptions would need a routing rig like theirs (174 measurements) to stay honest. No action beyond agentdocs-1 and agentdocs-7.

kept.title: Shared text: they inline it into every skill, we point to one references/ folder
kept.claim: Upstream edits shared text once in shared/ and copies it into every skill. scripts/sync_shared.py writes five blocks, about 1,229 words, into each SKILL.md. proposal-troubleshoot gets four, about 1,127 words, because it skips the report offer. guidelines.md (6,243 words) is copied into five skills, structure.json into eight and check.py into five. The copies keep each skill self-contained for skills.sh and per-skill installers, neither of which we use. Words loaded per run: their SKILL.md files run 2,290-5,643 words. Review plus guidelines is about 10,000 words. Supervise is about 11,900 with guidelines, or about 12,600 counting its closing-note and verifier-brief. Ours run 676-1,171, plus the checklist (2,877) and the brief or review shape (515 or 675): about 4,450 for design and 4,550 for review. Only design and review, plus check_proposal.py, read the checklist. Codex reached the checklist by the path relative to SKILL.md, which is our fallback. Text loaded into every session: their eleven descriptions total about 704 words. Our four total 183 words today and are hidden by disable-model-invocation. v3 lists them in Claude Code at about 70-75 words. Codex stays hidden pending the v3 test.
kept.recommendation: Keep ours. The plugin installs whole: both the Claude and Codex plugin caches hold references/. Four skills share one checklist, and the fallback path works in Codex. A sync script would maintain copies that no install path needs.

kept.title: Our steps carry Done-when criteria; theirs carry none
kept.claim: Each numbered step in design (8), review (7) and lit-search (4) carries a "Done when" criterion. Design step 7 and lit-search step 4 continue after that sentence, so not every step ends with it. The vendored ethics board has no numbered steps and no Done-when, only a Quality Checks list. None of their eleven SKILL.md files contains "done when". They mark completion at milestone level with the shared handoff ladder, plus prose stop rules: "run it again, until the only findings left are the ones the source caused", "Seed at convergence or when the user says enough", and "Verify before you report". Under the v3 spec's planned Agent run paragraph, which is not shipped yet, an agent caller would get a per-step exit test from ours. But a headless run stops early: design at step 6, with the brief left open, and review at step 5, with no fixes applied. So the Done-when criteria of design steps 7 and 8 and review step 6 can never be met in an agent run. Recommendation: keep ours, and have the Agent run paragraph (agentdocs-6) name the last step of each skill (design 6, review 5, lit-search 4) whose Done-when ends an agent run.
kept.recommendation: Keep ours. The only addition is the one in agentdocs-6: the Agent run paragraph names the step whose Done-when ends an agent run.

kept.title: Our pinned arxiv.py still queries over cleartext and parses the XML unchecked; upstream fixed both after the pin, under Security
kept.claim: Our nine vendored scripts match a38b7b1 byte for byte apart from the 4-line provenance header. At that pin, arxiv.py queries http://export.arxiv.org, so the query travels in cleartext before arXiv redirects. It also passes the whole response to ET.fromstring, catching only ParseError. Upstream commit a721bfd, released only in v0.9.0, changed four things. arXiv moves to HTTPS. A body is parsed only when its first markup is the Atom <feed> root, so no DOCTYPE or entity definition reaches expat. Nesting deeper than 32 is refused. The catch-all notes in search.py and snowball.py print the exception type instead of server text. Our copy has none of these, and the v3 wrapper design would pass the old notes through verbatim. The XML guard is defence in depth: local expat 2.6.1 already limits entity expansion, and ElementTree does not resolve external entities. The cleartext query and the leak of server text are the more concrete gaps. Two more post-pin commits touch the scripts: b311e4f (UTF-8 output) and b5d24b5 (a candidates/size line on stderr; snowball's per-seed default goes from 20 to 5). A re-vendor from v0.9.0 (tag object a60a9c5, commit 1666e69) brings in all three. Content changes in arxiv.py, common.py, search.py and snowball.py; the other five need only a new hash in their headers. The THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES pin row needs updating too. The cost is small: our SKILL.md passes --limit-per-seed 20 explicitly, and the key-file lookup is unchanged.
kept.recommendation: adopt: re-vendor all nine scripts from tag v0.9.0 (1666e69) into plugins/experiment-proposal/skills/lit-search/scripts/ with the same header form. Because the headers say do not hand-edit, re-vendoring is the only route to the fix.

kept.title: v3 keeps the scripts frozen at an untagged commit between releases; make the re-vendor to v0.9.0 a v3 task
kept.claim: v3 section 3 builds litsearch.py over scripts pinned at a38b7b1, which was never a release. It is 42 commits after v0.8.0 and was committed about five hours after v0.8.0 was tagged on 2026-10-13. Annotated release tags are not new upstream: v0.1.0 to v0.8.0 are all annotated, so a release was available when we pinned. What is new in 0.9.0 is the rule that main holds released versions only. The CHANGELOG that states this does not exist at v0.8.0. develop and main are both at 1666e69 (v0.9.0), so no unreleased work is waiting. v3 should re-vendor at v0.9.0 before writing the wrapper, and from now on pin only to a release tag, recording the tag beside the sha. This is not a header-only bump. Between a38b7b1 and v0.9.0, search.py and snowball.py start printing a `candidates: N (L lines, C characters on stdout)` line on stderr. snowball's default --limit-per-seed drops from 20 to 5, and it now prints each repeated note once. Exception notes give only the type name. arxiv moves to https through a new common.http_xml. YAML quoting (_yaml_scalar) does not change, so the lenient parse is still needed. Section 3's stderr summary should therefore be written against v0.9.0's output, and the wrapper should keep passing --limit-per-seed explicitly. The new scripts would pass the existing vendoring tests (write shapes, environment names, browser-verification heading), so the cost stays small. Do not strike "Vendored files untouched" from the Decisions row. Reword it to "re-vendored at v0.9.0, unchanged apart from headers", because the wrapper still does not patch the vendored scripts.
kept.recommendation: adopt: add a re-vendor step to v3 sections 3 and 4 at v0.9.0 (1666e69). It updates the sha in the nine headers, the hutzelmann row of OURS:plugins/experiment-proposal/THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md, the `pin a38b7b11` paragraph in OURS:ATTRIBUTION.md, and the HUTZELMANN constant in OURS:tests/test_experiment_proposal_plugin.py. Also strike "Vendored files untouched" from v3's lit-search Decisions row.

kept.title: v0.9.0 changes the stderr output and the snowball default that the v3 wrapper is designed around
kept.claim: Since the pin (a38b7b1 to 0.9.0), search.py and snowball.py both print a `candidates: N (L lines, C characters on stdout)` line on stderr just before the output. Above 25,000 characters or 1,800 lines the line ends with "— more than some hosts show from one command; run narrower". Upstream's SKILL.md says this line is for the agent and is not a degradation note to pass on. The catch-all notes in both scripts now give only the exception type. Only snowball.py prints each distinct note once per run; search.py never repeated notes. The SourceError `kind` `malformed_json` is now `malformed`, but this value never reaches stderr; the message still reads "returned malformed JSON". The 429 note is the same at both commits (`note: source degraded — <source>: HTTP 429`), so the v3 wrapper's `HTTP 429` substring trigger and a planted-429 test stub need no change. snowball.py's default `--limit-per-seed` went from 20 to 5: upstream measured 17,657 to 23,735 characters for one seed at 5, which fits under its 25,000-character bound, while two seeds at 5 go over it. Our SKILL.md:18 passes `--limit-per-seed 20` explicitly, which is the pin's default. Upstream's size reasoning (Claude Code shows up to 30,000 characters) applies to that call even now. The v3 wrapper passes `--limit-per-seed N` through and adds `--compact` and `--out`, which can reduce the risk. v3 plans no re-vendor. After a later re-vendor, though, the wrapper's step that echoes the vendored notes verbatim would pass on the `candidates:` line as if it were a degradation note. Its counts would describe the vendored stdout, not the wrapper's output after compacting, excluding and re-quoting. So the wrapper should skip lines that start with `candidates:`, or print its own count instead. SKILL.md should take the new per-seed default, one seed per call, when the vendored scripts are next updated.
kept.recommendation: adopt in v3 section 3. The wrapper's stderr parser should read or skip the `candidates:` line, and the 429 trigger should match the v0.9.0 note form. SKILL.md should drop the explicit `--limit-per-seed 20` (use the default 5, one seed per call). The unit test's planted-429 stub should emit stderr in the v0.9.0 form.

kept.title: The planned PR would add 429 backoff that upstream already has; the YAML bug it targets is still open at 1666e69
kept.claim: At the pin (a38b7b1) and at HEAD (1666e69), upstream common.py retries HTTP 429 twice, waiting 3 s and then 6 s, and our vendored Semantic Scholar client says it does. The "adds 429 backoff" half of the planned PR therefore duplicates what upstream already has. What upstream lacks for the shared Semantic Scholar pool is a longer wait, or one that honours Retry-After. The YAML half is still needed. `_yaml_scalar` quotes a value only when it matches a fixed pattern (certain characters, leading or trailing whitespace, a leading - or ?, or an empty value). An embedded line break does not match, and even the quoted branch escapes only backslash and double quote. Our own output proves this is the cause: snow1.yaml lines 2711-2713 hold an unquoted title broken by newlines (DOI 10.7717/peerj-cs.4052). The PR must escape line breaks and control characters, not just quote, and must change both upstream copies of `_yaml_scalar`: skills/proposal-lit-search/scripts/common.py and skills/proposal-reverse/scripts/common.py.
kept.recommendation: adopt: rewrite v3 section 3's upstream line. The PR quotes and escapes any scalar containing a line break or control character in `_yaml_scalar`. Drop the 429 part, or propose it as a separate change for Semantic Scholar (a longer or Retry-After-aware wait) backed by our measured 429s. Keep the wrapper's own 20/40/80 s backoff.

kept.title: v3's planned PR and issue do not follow upstream's contribution rules
kept.claim: The v3 plan for upstream (one PR for YAML quoting plus 429 backoff, one issue for DBLP) ignores upstream's contribution rules, and the spec mentions none of them. Those rules are: open an issue first (README.md:225); target develop; a behaviour change needs an OpenSpec change folder made with their CLI (AGENTS.md:13), whose proposal.md ends with a `Changelog:` line; `uv run poe test` must pass; and only sync sources may be edited. common.py in proposal-lit-search is a sync source copied into proposal-import and proposal-reverse, so a fix there regenerates three skills. The skill-defect form needs an installed skill and a proposal-troubleshoot report, but blank issues are enabled, so our report should be a blank issue. Two changes to the spec's plan: (a) 429 retry and backoff already exist at a38b7b1 and at HEAD (RETRY_CODES = (429, 500, 502, 503), BACKOFF_SECONDS), so the PR should carry only the quoting fix, unless we propose a different retry policy for Semantic Scholar's repeated 429s. (b) The bug still exists at HEAD: `_yaml_scalar` is identical, `entry()` only calls `title.strip()`, and the quoting regex never checks for an embedded newline, so a title containing one is written unquoted across lines. The test fixture should be a minimal synthetic entry in the style of test_lit_common.py, a title with an embedded newline. The reason is minimality, not privacy. snow1.yaml holds public paper metadata, not proposal text, and upstream's own test data contains real API responses with real author names.
kept.recommendation: adopt in v3 section 3. First open two blank issues, one for the DBLP empty results and one for YAML quoting. Each states that we vendor the scripts and was reproduced against v0.9.0, not a38b7b1. Then open one PR per behaviour change, targeting develop. Each carries an openspec/changes/<id>/ folder ending with `Changelog: ...`, a synthetic fixture (their `Erika Musterfrau` convention), and edits to skills/proposal-lit-search/scripts/common.py plus the copies scripts/sync_shared.py regenerates. Our 0.3.0 does not wait on either.

kept.title: Nothing tests our claim that the scripts are unchanged apart from their headers; upstream refuses drifted copies at commit and in CI
kept.claim: THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES and ATTRIBUTION say the nine lit-search scripts are unchanged apart from their headers. That is true today: each body matches upstream at a38b7b1 exactly once the 4-line header after the shebang is removed. But no automated check enforces it. Our tests check the provenance header strings, the exact file list, that each script compiles, that `--help` runs offline, that no script writes files or imports research_vault, and which environment names the scripts read. None of them compares a script body with the upstream file at the pin, and the v3 spec says 'vendored files untouched' without specifying a check. Upstream's pre-commit hook and CI (`sync_shared.py --check`) re-render every generated copy from its in-repo source and refuse the commit or fail the build when the text differs. That is a same-repo sync check, not a vendoring check. For copies taken from another repository at a pin, the equivalent is a recorded digest. Our repo already has a sha256-in-JSON pin of this shape (.github/okf-pin.json), but that pin detects upstream SPEC.md moving away from the pin, not our local copy being edited. Recording each script's upstream sha256 and testing the de-headered body against it would close the gap at small cost. The two mdformat-normalised Markdown files carry local edits, so their own body hash can catch later hand edits but cannot show they match upstream.
kept.recommendation: adopt: for each of the nine scripts, record the sha256 of the upstream file at the pin, either in the test's VENDORED dict or in a pin JSON beside THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES. Add a test that strips the 4-line header and compares the hash. For the two mdformat-normalised Markdown files, record our own body hash at vendoring time. The governance-2 re-vendor then updates one table.

kept.title: We have no changelog, so users cannot see what 0.2.0 changed or what 0.3.0 will change or break
kept.claim: Upstream keeps a Keep a Changelog file that says what each version part means. Breaking entries start with **Breaking:**, and nearly every entry links its OpenSpec change folder; a few cite a commit hash instead (for example 7385be1 and 4a11adb), and at least one cites nothing. Releases that predate the file got retroactive sections, and their tags were cut on 2026-10-14, the same time the file was added. We have two annotated tags whose messages hold only the version string, plus plugin.json. What changed per version lives only in specs, eval records and commit messages. v3 section 4 lists README and plugin.json edits but no release notes, although 0.3.0 makes the skills model-invocable and changes what `--references` checks and prints.
kept.recommendation: adopt: add plugins/experiment-proposal/CHANGELOG.md. Sections 0.1.0 and 0.2.0 are retroactive, each naming its tag and spec. Section 0.3.0 comes from v3's Decisions table and states that 0.2.0 briefs stay valid. Add the file to v3 section 4 and to the README's Version section, plus a test that every `experiment-proposal--v*` tag has a section. Skip their changelog.py, union-merge and release-command machinery.

kept.title: v3's ethics-board edits leave the notices, ATTRIBUTION and a test describing the old single edit, and override a v2 non-goal without naming it
kept.claim: v3 removes `disable-model-invocation: true` from the vendored the-ethics-board and shortens its description (section 1, line 40, "with the provenance comment updated"). It also adds a marked two-line edit to the upstream body (section 4, line 78), and that edit names no record update. THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES, ATTRIBUTION and the provenance header all describe a single frontmatter edit that adds the flag; the header also says "Do not hand-edit this file". test_the_ethics_board_gains_only_the_marked_invocation_edit asserts the flag is present. Among these records, v3 names only the provenance comment, and only for the frontmatter edits. It never mentions NOTICES (except as unchanged for lit-search), ATTRIBUTION or this test, although v2 explicitly named the NOTICES and ATTRIBUTION updates when hci-researcher gained an edit. The body edit overrides v2's non-goal "Editing vendored text beyond marked frontmatter edits" without naming it, while v3 states that every v2 decision it does not name still stands. Upstream keeps an explicit list of its deliberate divergences from the Agent Skills standard (a looser analog than vendored-text edits) and treats any unlisted divergence as a defect.
kept.recommendation: adopt in v3 sections 1 and 4: name the v2 non-goal that v3 overrides, and update the pm-claude-skills row of THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES, ATTRIBUTION's pm-claude-skills paragraph, the provenance header, and test_the_ethics_board_gains_only_the_marked_invocation_edit to describe the edits v3 actually makes.

kept.title: Change process: their archived OpenSpec folders versus our superseding design specs; borrow the closing Changelog line and a landed status
kept.claim: Upstream runs behaviour changes as OpenSpec folders (proposal, design, tasks, spec deltas). Each is archived under a date prefix and merged into living specs under openspec/specs/. 175 changes are archived, and the one read here (2026-10-13-classify-arxiv-answers) runs to 8,056 words across four files. We write one design spec per release that supersedes the last "where it changes it", plus a plan and eval records. The full OpenSpec loop is too heavy for a one-author plugin, but two parts are cheap.
